items.text: Loss of interest or pleasure in almost everything
items.why: Anhedonia is a core MDD symptom; it isn't on the PDD list.

items.text: Slowing of movement others can see
items.why: Psychomotor change is an MDD criterion, not a PDD one.

items.text: Recurrent thoughts of death or suicide
items.why: In the MDD list; PDD's list has hopelessness but not suicidal thoughts.

items.text: Five or more symptoms in the same period
items.why: MDD's count. PDD needs only two extra symptoms.

items.text: Depressed mood on more days than not
items.why: PDD's wording; MDD says most of the day, nearly every day.

items.text: Never symptom-free for more than 2 months
In children, 1 year is enough
items.why: PDD shortens to 1 year in children and adolescents.

items.text: Low self-esteem and hopelessness for years
items.why: Two of PDD's six symptoms, over the long haul.

items.why: Marked impairment separates mania from hypomania.

Never had a full mood episode

At least 2 years (1 in young people)

Muscle tension and tiring easily

DUEL.vignette: A 30-year-old has felt low, tired and hopeless for three weeks since a breakup. She still enjoys films with friends and eats and sleeps normally.
features: Too few symptoms for a depressive episode, after a clear stressor
Low mood for at least 2 years
Worry about many topics for 6 months
A past hypomanic episode
DUEL.why: Low mood after a stressor with only a few symptoms is adjustment disorder; MDD needs 5+ symptoms for 2 weeks.
DUEL.objective: Tell adjustment disorder from a depressive episode.

DUEL.vignette: A 38-year-old says he has been gloomy 'for as long as I can remember', more days than not for six years, with low energy and poor self-esteem.
features: Low mood more days than not for 2+ years
5+ symptoms for 2 weeks
Hypomanic spells too
Started within 3 months of a stressor
DUEL.why: Persistent depressive disorder: low mood more days than not for at least 2 years.
DUEL.objective: Use the 2-year rule for persistent depressive disorder.

DUEL.vignette: A 26-year-old has had two depressions. Last spring she had five days of little sleep, fast talk and big plans; she kept working and friends noticed.
features: A 4-day hypomanic episode without marked impairment
A week-long high needing admission
Never any high
Symptoms always below full episodes
DUEL.why: Hypomania (4+ days, no marked impairment) plus major depression = bipolar II.
DUEL.objective: Spot hypomania plus depression as bipolar II.

DUEL.vignette: A 24-year-old is admitted after eight days of no sleep, spending his savings and saying he is chosen to lead the nation.
features: A manic episode of a week or needing admission
A high of only 4 days
6 months of continuous psychosis
Started during heavy drug use
DUEL.why: Mania (1 week, or any length if admitted) defines bipolar I.

DUEL.vignette: A 33-year-old has sudden surges of terror with chest pain at random times, then a month of worrying about the next one.
features: Unexpected attacks plus a month of worry about more
Worry about many topics for 6 months
Health worry with few or no symptoms
Fear of one specific trigger
DUEL.why: Panic disorder: recurrent unexpected attacks and at least a month of worry or change in behaviour.

DUEL.vignette: A 41-year-old worries daily about money, work, her children and her health. She can't switch it off, feels tense and sleeps badly. It's been a year.
features: Hard-to-control worry about many things for 6+ months
Sudden attacks that peak in minutes
Intrusive thoughts with rituals
Two weeks of low mood and anhedonia
DUEL.why: GAD: excessive, hard-to-control worry about many topics for 6 months with body symptoms.

DUEL.vignette: A 20-year-old dreads class presentations because others will see him shake and think he's stupid. With close friends he's fine.
features: Fear of being judged when watched, not pervasive inadequacy
Lifelong feeling of inferiority in all relationships
Attacks out of the blue
Difficulty with social communication itself
DUEL.why: Social anxiety disorder centres on fear of scrutiny; avoidant PD is a pervasive pattern of inadequacy.
DUEL.objective: Separate social anxiety from avoidant personality.

DUEL.vignette: A 27-year-old checks the gas knob 30 times before leaving, fearing a fire. She knows it's excessive and hates the thoughts.
features: Unwanted intrusive thoughts with rituals to reduce distress
Rules and perfectionism that feel right
Worry about many real-life topics
Fear of having a serious illness
DUEL.why: OCD obsessions are ego-dystonic and drive compulsions; OCPD traits feel right to the person.
DUEL.objective: Separate OCD from OCPD by insight.

DUEL.vignette: A 45-year-old manager redoes every report until it's perfect, won't delegate and insists on his rules at home. He thinks everyone else is careless.
features: Perfectionism and control that feel right to him
Intrusive thoughts he wants to stop
Grandiosity and need for admiration
Clutter from not discarding
DUEL.why: OCPD: pervasive perfectionism and control, ego-syntonic, without true obsessions.

DUEL.vignette: A 21-year-old spends hours checking her jawline in mirrors, sure it's lopsided. Others see nothing wrong. She eats normally.
features: Preoccupation with a defect in looks others can't see
Fear of weight gain with low weight
Fear of being judged generally
A fixed belief outside appearance
DUEL.why: Body dysmorphic disorder; when the belief is about appearance, use BDD even with absent insight.

lines: How have you been feeling these days?
...(long pause)... Nothing is left for me, doctor. Everything is grey.
Do you ever think about death?
Sometimes I wish I would just not wake up. I have not thought how. My daughter's wedding is in March.
EXCERPTS.note: Sits slumped, hardly moves his hands. Answers come after long gaps, in a quiet, flat voice.

findings.q: Sits slumped, hardly moves his hands
findings.why: Slow, few movements with a slumped posture is psychomotor slowing, typical of moderate to severe depression.

findings.q: Answers come after long gaps, in a quiet, flat voice
findings.why: The words do come, but slowly and quietly after long gaps. That is increased latency. Poverty of speech means very few words, not slow ones.

findings.q: Nothing is left for me, doctor. Everything is grey.
findings.why: This is his own description of how he feels, so it is mood (subjective). It is a metaphor, not a fixed belief that the world is gone.

findings.q: Sometimes I wish I would just not wake up. I have not thought how.
findings.why: A wish to be dead with no method or plan is a passive death wish. It still needs a full risk check; the wedding is a protective factor worth noting.

EXCERPTS.objective: Recognise Psychomotor slowing and Slowed speech, long pauses

lines: Tonight, tonight, the night is young and so am I! I've designed forty dresses since Sunday, Milan wants me, Paris too, I don't need sleep, sleep is for people without a destiny!
Fantastic! Best I've ever felt in my life!
EXCERPTS.note: Talks fast and loudly; hard to interrupt. Laughing, over-familiar, touches the doctor's arm.

findings.q: Talks fast and loudly; hard to interrupt
findings.why: Fast, loud and hard to interrupt is pressured speech, a key sign of mania.

findings.q: Best I've ever felt in my life!
findings.why: Her own words describe feeling on top of the world: elated mood.

findings.q: Laughing, over-familiar, touches the doctor's arm
findings.why: What you see matches her elation and goes beyond the situation: elated, expansive affect. It is not incongruent, because it fits what she says.
A belief of special fame with no basis, held in mania, is a grandiose delusion (confirm it is fixed and false by checking with family).

EXCERPTS.objective: Recognise Pressured speech and Elated mood

lines: What did you have for breakfast?

Well, the milkman came late, as he does on Tuesdays because his cousin runs the Lanka route, and my wife, who taught Hindi for thirty-one years, by the way, boiled the milk twice, she always does, and so, to answer you, poha.
EXCERPTS.note: Pleasant, detailed. Takes a long road but always arrives. Clean kurta, well groomed.

findings.q: and so, to answer you, poha
findings.why: Lots of needless detail, but the answer arrives. That is circumstantiality. Tangential speech would never get back to breakfast.
Well kempt: a normal finding that also helps rate his self-care in a memory assessment.

EXCERPTS.objective: Place Circumstantial and Well kempt, appropriate in the right domains

lines: Exams are kind of like hockey seasons, you know? My brother plays hockey. His coach is from Sweden. Sweden has amazing design, all those furniture stores...
Oh, the furniture there is so cheap, my roommate bought a lamp...
EXCERPTS.note: Speaks at a normal speed. Each step is linked to the last, but she never returns to the question.

findings.q: Oh, the furniture there is so cheap, my roommate bought a lamp
findings.why: Each step links to the last, at normal speed, but she never gets back to the exams, even when redirected. That is tangential. With fast, pressured jumps it would be flight of ideas.
Rate is normal. That is one reason this is tangentiality rather than flight of ideas.

EXCERPTS.objective: Place Tangential and Normal rate, tone and volume in the right domains

lines: I hear my wife's voice, saying 'have you eaten?' It is inside my head, not in the room. I know it is my mind missing her.
Does it feel like a real voice coming through your ears?
No. Clear, but inside. It comes on its own.
EXCERPTS.note: Fully alert. Grieving for six months. No other psychotic features.

findings.q: It is inside my head, not in the room. I know it is my mind missing her.
findings.why: Vivid and involuntary, but in inner space and known not to be a real perception, in clear consciousness: a pseudo-hallucination (Jaspers). Common in grief and not, by itself, a sign of psychosis.
Clear consciousness matters: Jaspers' pseudo-hallucinations are seen in full consciousness.

EXCERPTS.objective: Tell Pseudo-hallucination apart from Second-person voice

CAMPAIGNS.title: First voices
CAMPAIGNS.blurb: His parents bring him in: he has stopped attending class, barely eats the hostel food and talks to someone who isn't there.

beats.text: Aditya sits with his hood up, eyes on the door. His father does the talking: 'He was a topper. For months now he locks his room and says his roommates are against him.'
His mother adds quietly that he smokes ganja with friends, 'but only sometimes'.

options.text: Tell him early that this sounds like schizophrenia so he knows what he's dealing with.
options.why: A label in the first minutes, before a full assessment, frightens and alienates. It is also often premature: first-episode psychosis has many causes.

options.text: Start with a urine drug test before talking, so you know what you're dealing with.
options.why: Testing is useful, but leading with it feels like an accusation and costs trust.

options.text: See Aditya alone first, then the parents. Open questions about what has been happening, in his words.
options.why: Seeing him alone protects trust and lets him say things he can't say in front of his father. You still hear the family afterwards.

options.text: Keep the parents in the room the whole time so nothing is missed.
options.why: Collateral history matters, but a suspicious young man may say nothing in front of his parents.

decisions.prompt: Before he leaves today, what must you cover?

options.text: His full childhood and developmental history; risk can wait till next time.
options.why: A thorough history is good, but risk can't wait. Unasked questions are unmanaged risks.

options.text: Request a brain scan and blood tests, and book a longer session for the rest.
options.why: Ruling out medical causes is right, but you have left today without asking about danger.

options.text: A risk check: thoughts of harming himself or anyone else, voices that give orders, and whether he feels safe at the hostel. Plus a physical check and drug screen.
options.why: Psychosis risk lives in the content: who he fears, what the voices say, what he might do to protect himself. Medical causes and substances must be ruled out early.

beats.text: This time Aditya talks. The voices are two men who comment on everything he does. He believes his roommates are adding poison to the mess food, so he eats only biscuits.
Aditya says almost nothing. His mother tells you he has lost weight and eats only sealed biscuit packets.
His blood tests and scan are normal. The drug screen is positive for cannabis.

decisions.prompt: The psychiatrist asks your view on medicine. What do you suggest?

options.text: A low dose of a second-generation antipsychotic, increased slowly, with weight, sugar and lipids checked from the start.
options.why: First-episode patients respond to lower doses and are more sensitive to side effects. Planning metabolic checks early protects his long-term health and his willingness to continue.

options.text: A high dose so the voices stop fast and he can return to class.
options.why: High doses in a first episode bring stiffness, restlessness and sedation without faster recovery. Side effects are the top reason young people stop.

options.text: No medicine for now; talking therapy only.
options.why: Psychological work matters, but untreated psychosis with poor eating and fear of poisoning carries real risk. Therapy works best alongside medicine here.

options.text: Mix it into his food at home so he doesn't refuse.
options.why: Covert medication without legal process breaks trust and his rights. If he finds out, he may never engage again.

decisions.prompt: How do you explain what is happening?

options.text: Use his own words: 'Your brain is under great stress and is making real-sounding voices. Many people recover well.' Ask what he makes of it.
options.why: Starting from his experience, using stress and vulnerability, and holding hope builds insight without a fight.

options.text: Give him a printed leaflet about schizophrenia to read later.
options.why: Leaflets help as a follow-up, not as the explanation. He may not read it, or may read the label and panic.

options.text: Tell him firmly the voices aren't real and he must stop believing them.
options.why: Arguing with a delusion hardens it and costs trust. Curiosity works better than confrontation.

chapters.title: Session 3 · Ganja and a phone call

beats.text: Before the session, the hostel warden calls: last night Aditya held a knife at his door, shouting at his roommate to 'stop the poison'. No one was hurt.
Because you asked about his fears early, a safety plan is already in place: he moved to a cousin's flat and texts his mother each night.
He admits he smokes ganja most nights 'to calm the voices'. It helps for an hour, then they get louder.

options.text: Same-day review with the psychiatrist. Talk with Aditya and his family about a short admission to keep everyone safe, and a plan for the knife.
options.why: Acting on a fear-driven threat with a weapon is urgent. A brief admission can be the safest, kindest step, done with him wherever possible.

options.text: Keep the routine appointment next month; nobody was hurt.
options.why: 'Nobody was hurt' is luck. Risk rises when fear and a weapon meet.

options.text: Call the police to arrest him.
options.why: Police may be needed in danger, but this moment needs a health response first.

decisions.prompt: How do you handle the cannabis?

options.text: Warn him you'll tell his parents unless he stops today.
options.why: Threats push use underground and wreck trust.

options.text: Explore it with him: what he gets from it, what it costs, how it links to the voices. Agree a goal he chooses, like cutting down first.
options.why: A motivational approach respects his choice and links cannabis to his own goals. Continued use raises relapse risk in psychosis.

options.text: Leave it; one problem at a time.
options.why: Cannabis is driving his voices. Ignoring it leaves a known risk running.

beats.text: His father: 'He's just become lazy and spoilt. In my time we didn't have depression and all.' His mother: 'We took him to a healer at the temple. Is this black magic?'
His father keeps checking his phone and talks over Aditya. Aditya stares at the floor.

decisions.prompt: How do you run the meeting?

options.text: Explain psychosis plainly, ask about their beliefs without mocking them, and show how calm, low-criticism support helps recovery. Agree early warning signs together.
options.why: Family work cuts relapse. High criticism at home (high 'expressed emotion') predicts relapse. Respecting their beliefs keeps them on side.

options.text: Tell them black magic is superstition and they must stop visiting the healer.
options.why: Dismissing their framework makes them choose between you and their faith. Many families use both; work alongside it.

options.text: Skip the meeting: he's an adult and can manage alone.
options.why: Adults keep their right to privacy, but with his consent family support is one of the strongest protective factors.

options.text: Tell the parents their strictness caused this.
options.why: Blame is false and destroys the alliance. Families don't cause psychosis.

decisions.prompt: He wants to go back to college. What do you set up?

options.text: Tell the college his diagnosis so they keep an eye on him.
options.why: Sharing without consent breaches confidentiality and can lead to stigma.

options.text: With his consent, refer to an early-intervention team and occupational therapy, and write to the college for a lighter, step-by-step return.
options.why: Specialist early-intervention care improves outcomes. A graded return protects his future and his self-belief.

options.text: Advise him to drop out for a year to rest.
options.why: Long inactivity and loss of role worsen outcomes. Most can return with support.

beats.text: Aditya shuffles in, stiff, his hands trembling. 'These tablets make me a robot. I stopped them three days ago.'
The voices are quieter, he eats in the mess again, and he has gained some weight.
He has missed many doses. 'I feel fine, why take them?'

decisions.prompt: What do you raise with the psychiatrist?

options.text: He feels fine, so suggest stopping medicine now.
options.why: Stopping soon after a first episode carries a high relapse risk. Any stop should be planned and slow.

options.text: Tell him to keep taking it exactly as before.
options.why: Ignoring side effects is the fastest route to stopping.

options.text: Ask about every side effect, share them with the psychiatrist to adjust the dose or switch, and keep the weight and sugar checks going.
options.why: Side effects named and acted on keep people on treatment. Weight gain is common with several antipsychotics and needs watching.

decisions.prompt: Last task: what does he leave with?

options.text: A written relapse plan with him and his family: his early signs (poor sleep, suspicion), who to call, and his cannabis goal.
options.why: A relapse plan made together turns warning signs into action before a crisis.

options.text: 'See you in six months.'
options.why: Early psychosis needs close follow-up; relapse is common in the first years.

endings.title: Back in class
endings.text: Aditya returns to college on a lighter timetable. He knows his early signs and texts his team when sleep slips. His father now drives him to appointments.

endings.title: Steady, but fragile
endings.text: The voices are quieter, but he takes medicine on and off, and home is tense. One bad month could tip him back.

endings.title: Readmitted
endings.text: Within the year Aditya is admitted after a frightening relapse. The trust you needed was never built; the next team has to start again.

tags.objective: Assess and engage a young man with first-episode psychosis and cannabis use, with his family.

CAMPAIGNS.title: The quiet house
CAMPAIGNS.blurb: At her daughter's vaccination visit the nurse notices Divya hasn't smiled once. Her husband works in Bengaluru on weekdays.

beats.text: Divya holds the baby stiffly. 'I don't feel anything for her. I cry when everyone sleeps. My mother-in-law says it's the baby blues.' Her daughter is a month old.

options.text: Find a private room. Use a postnatal depression screen, then ask her directly, kindly, about thoughts of harming herself or the baby.
options.why: Baby blues are brief and settle on their own soon after birth; this has lasted too long. Direct questions about harm, asked kindly, don't plant ideas and often bring relief.

options.text: Agree that it's baby blues and say it will pass.
options.why: Baby blues are short and mild. Persistent low mood and no feeling for the baby suggest postnatal depression.

options.text: Book her in with a psychologist for next month.
options.why: A referral is reasonable, but you haven't checked her safety today.

decisions.prompt: She whispers: 'I keep seeing myself dropping her from the balcony. I would never! I've stopped bathing her in case I do something.' How do you read this?

options.text: These sound like unwanted, horrifying intrusive thoughts she resists. Such thoughts rarely lead to harm, but you still check for confusion, voices or strange beliefs, and her own suicide risk.
options.why: Ego-dystonic intrusive thoughts (she hates them, avoids the baby to be safe) are common after birth and differ from psychotic ideas. Postpartum psychosis is rarer, comes on fast and is an emergency.

options.text: 'Everyone has thoughts like that. Ignore them.' Move on.
options.why: Normalising helps, but stopping there skips the checks for psychosis and her own risk, and leaves her alone with the fear.

options.text: Call child protection now and arrange for the baby to be taken from her.
options.why: This misreads OCD-type thoughts as intent, punishes her for being honest and makes it less likely she'll ever disclose again.

beats.text: Divya looks lighter: 'You told me I'm not a monster. I bathed her yesterday with my mother-in-law beside me.'
Divya has lost weight. She sleeps two hours a night even when the baby sleeps.
She asks: 'If I take tablets, can I still feed her?'

decisions.prompt: What do you discuss with the psychiatrist?

options.text: Suggest valproate to steady her mood.
options.why: Valproate is not a treatment for postnatal depression and is avoided in women who could become pregnant because of serious risks to a baby.

options.text: An antidepressant with good breastfeeding data (sertraline is a common choice), weighing benefits and risks with her, alongside psychological therapy.
options.why: Some antidepressants pass into milk in only tiny amounts; sertraline has some of the most reassuring data. Untreated depression also harms mother and baby.

options.text: Tell her she must stop breastfeeding to take any medicine.
options.why: Usually unnecessary, and stopping feeding against her wishes can deepen guilt.

options.text: Avoid all medicine because she is breastfeeding.
options.why: With moderate to severe symptoms, avoiding treatment carries its own risk.

decisions.prompt: How do you explain postnatal depression?

options.text: Tell her to count her blessings: she has a healthy baby.
options.why: Minimising adds guilt to depression.

options.text: 'This is a common, treatable illness after birth, not weakness or bad mothering. Most women recover fully.' Explain the intrusive thoughts too.
options.why: Removing shame is half the treatment. Naming it as common and treatable builds hope and insight.

beats.text: Her mother-in-law comes: 'She's weak. In our time we managed. And she must stay inside, eat what I give, no visitors.' Divya says nothing.

decisions.prompt: How do you work with the family?

options.text: Tell them the customs are harmful and Divya needs freedom.
options.why: Attacking customs alienates the people doing the caring.

options.text: Speak only to the husband by phone and leave the mother-in-law out.
options.why: He matters, but the mother-in-law is at home every day. Leaving her out wastes the main source of support.

options.text: Honour the confinement customs that help (rest, food, help with the baby), and ask that someone takes one night feed with expressed milk so Divya gets a stretch of sleep.
options.why: Working with tradition, not against it, gets the family on board. Protected sleep is one of the most powerful levers in postnatal depression.

beats.text: Her husband calls at 11 pm: Divya said 'the baby would be better off without me' and searched online for tablet overdoses.
Divya is sleeping better. She took the baby to the temple and smiled at a neighbour's joke.

options.text: Tell him to bring her to the next routine appointment.
options.why: A new, specific suicide plan needs action today.

options.text: Same-day assessment with the psychiatrist. With the family, lock away medicines at home, agree who stays with her, and write a safety plan. If risk is high, discuss a mother-and-baby unit.
options.why: Thoughts that the baby is better off without her are a serious sign. Removing means and never leaving her alone are life-saving steps; a mother-baby unit keeps them together.

decisions.prompt: Where should her ongoing care sit?

options.text: A perinatal mental health service for therapy (CBT for depression and the intrusive thoughts), plus a local new-mothers group.
options.why: Specialist perinatal care and peer support cut isolation and treat the thoughts directly.

options.text: Refer only to a faith healer, as the family prefers.
options.why: Faith can sit beside care, but not replace it when risk is present.

beats.text: Divya is feeding the baby, laughing more. 'I feel like myself. Can I stop the tablets now?'
Divya is coping, just. 'I still wake at 3 am with my heart racing.'

decisions.prompt: What do you advise she discusses with the psychiatrist?

options.text: Stop now since she feels well.
options.why: Early stopping is the commonest cause of relapse.

options.text: Keep going for a good while after feeling well, then plan a slow taper together.
options.why: Stopping soon after recovery raises relapse risk; a planned, gradual stop avoids discontinuation symptoms.

decisions.prompt: She asks about a second baby someday.

options.text: Explain that postnatal depression can return, and plan early support for any future pregnancy: tell the team early, line up sleep help.
options.why: Risk of recurrence is real, and a plan made when well is far easier to follow.

options.text: Advise her never to have another child.
options.why: That's not your decision to make, and with planning most women do well.

endings.title: Two cups of filter coffee
endings.text: Divya and her mother-in-law share the early feed. Divya bathes her daughter every morning and is back to sketching. She knows the plan if the darkness returns.

endings.title: Getting there
endings.text: Divya is better but tired and alone on weekdays. Some days the thoughts creep back. Support at home is patchy.

endings.title: A hard year
endings.text: Divya's depression drags on for most of the year, with a crisis admission. The family feels blamed and stops coming.

tags.objective: Tell intrusive thoughts from psychosis after birth and treat postnatal depression safely.

ROOMS.title: The night shift
ROOMS.patient: Mr Sen, 52, three days after a fractured leg
ROOMS.intro: 2 am. The nurse calls: Mr Sen is shouting, pulling at his drip and brushing 'insects' off his blanket. The ward doors lock until the team solves his case.
ROOMS.outro: Mr Sen settles over the next days. Thiamine went in first, his withdrawal was treated safely, and before discharge he agreed to meet the de-addiction team.

puzzles.prompt: Observation note: 'Thinks it is morning and that he is at the railway office. Drifts off mid-sentence, then is suddenly alert. Says beetles are crawling on the sheet. Sweating, hands shaking.' Tick every MSE finding.
options: Formal thought disorder in clear consciousness
puzzles.hint: Three findings. Look for orientation, attention and what he sees.
puzzles.why: Disorientation, fluctuating attention and vivid visual hallucinations point to a clouded consciousness. That is delirium until proved otherwise.
puzzles.unlock: His wife, on the phone: 'He drinks a full bottle of rum every night. He hasn't had a drop since the accident.'

tags.objective: Pick out the MSE signs of delirium.

puzzles.prompt: Confused, hallucinating, shaking, three days after his last drink. Most likely diagnosis?
puzzles.hint: Count back from the last drink.
puzzles.why: Delirium with tremor, sweating and vivid hallucinations a few days after stopping heavy drinking is delirium tremens, a medical emergency.
puzzles.unlock: On examination: when he looks to the side, his eyes jerk and won't move fully. He staggers when he stands.

tags.objective: Recognise delirium tremens from timing and signs.

puzzles.prompt: Eye movement problems and an unsteady walk, in a heavy drinker. What else is going on?
options: A stroke of the frontal lobe
puzzles.why: Confusion, eye movement problems and ataxia is the classic triad of Wernicke's encephalopathy, caused by thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency. Often only one or two signs are present, so suspect it in every heavy drinker.
puzzles.unlock: Pulse 124, temperature 38.2, blood pressure high. The night doctor wants to start a glucose drip because he hasn't eaten.

tags.objective: Spot Wernicke's encephalopathy in a heavy drinker.

puzzles.prompt: Which dangers are real tonight? Tick all.
options: Permanent memory damage if thiamine is missed
Becoming addicted to his first benzodiazepine dose
Suicide with saved-up tablets at home
puzzles.hint: Four of them belong to tonight, on this ward.
puzzles.why: Delirium tremens can kill through seizures, injury, dehydration and heart strain. Untreated Wernicke's can leave permanent memory loss (Korsakoff syndrome). A short supervised benzodiazepine course is the treatment, not the danger.
puzzles.unlock: The ward sister asks: 'Which came first? I need it for the handover.'

tags.objective: Name the real dangers of severe alcohol withdrawal.

puzzles.prompt: Put alcohol withdrawal in the order it usually unfolds after the last drink.
puzzles.hint: It starts mild, within hours, and ends with the most dangerous.
puzzles.why: Tremor comes first, within hours. Perceptual disturbances follow, then seizures, and delirium tremens usually arrives within about three days. Some people skip steps, so watch closely from the start.
puzzles.unlock: The glucose drip is hanging, ready to go.

tags.objective: Order the stages of alcohol withdrawal.

puzzles.prompt: The drip is ready. What must happen first?
options: Give thiamine into a vein before any glucose
Start the glucose now and thiamine tomorrow
Hold thiamine until a blood level comes back
puzzles.hint: Glucose burns up the little B1 he has left.
puzzles.why: Glucose metabolism uses thiamine. Giving glucose first can tip a deficient brain into Wernicke's. In suspected Wernicke's, thiamine goes in by injection, in high doses, before or with glucose.
puzzles.unlock: Blood results: his liver is badly damaged (cirrhosis on scan, low albumin).

puzzles.prompt: His liver is failing. Which benzodiazepine is the safer choice for the withdrawal?
puzzles.hint: Which one skips the liver's slow, oxidative step?
puzzles.why: Lorazepam is cleared by a simple liver step (glucuronidation) and has no long-acting active metabolites, so it is less likely to build up in liver failure. Diazepam and chlordiazepoxide are long-acting and can accumulate. Antipsychotics alone don't treat withdrawal and lower the seizure threshold.

tags.objective: Choose a benzodiazepine for withdrawal in liver failure.

ROOMS.title: The still room
ROOMS.intro: Transferred from a private hospital: she has not spoken, eaten or moved from her bed for four days. The ward is locked until the team works out why.
ROOMS.outro: After lorazepam Ms Lakshmi sipped water and whispered her name. With the depression treated, she was back in her classroom months later.

puzzles.prompt: Observation note: 'Lies still, staring. No answer to questions. When I raised her arm it stayed in the air for minutes, then she resisted my moving it, like soft wax. Pulls away when asked to open her mouth.' Tick every finding.
options: Catalepsy (holds a posture she is put in)
puzzles.hint: Four. The last two would need her to be talking.
puzzles.why: Mutism, catalepsy, waxy flexibility and negativism are all catatonic signs. Staring and immobility (stupor) often sit alongside.
puzzles.unlock: Her sister says: for two months before this she cried every night, stopped eating and said she was a burden.

puzzles.prompt: Catatonic signs after two months of low mood. Best formulation?
options: Catatonia associated with major depressive disorder
puzzles.hint: Catatonia is a syndrome; it sits on top of something.
puzzles.why: Catatonia can come with depression, mania, psychosis or medical illness. Here the months of low mood, guilt and poor eating point to depression. Mood disorders are among its commonest causes.
puzzles.unlock: The transfer letter: 'Given haloperidol injection twice, as she was not responding.' Now: temperature 39, she is rigid all over and sweating. CK (a muscle enzyme) is very high.

tags.objective: Diagnosis: Catatonic signs after two months of low mood.

puzzles.prompt: Fever, rigidity, sweating and a high CK after haloperidol. What must you rule out now?
puzzles.why: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (fever, rigidity, unstable pulse and blood pressure, confusion, raised CK) can follow antipsychotics, and catatonia raises the risk. Serotonin syndrome brings jerky reflexes rather than lead-pipe rigidity, after serotonin medicines.
puzzles.unlock: The physician confirms: haloperidol is stopped, fluids started. She is still not eating or moving.

tags.objective: Differential: Fever, rigidity, sweating and a high CK after haloperidol.

puzzles.prompt: She hasn't moved, eaten or drunk for days. Which risks need action? Tick all.
options: Clots in the legs that can travel to the lungs
Violence to staff as the main risk
Addiction to lorazepam within a day
puzzles.hint: Think of what lying still and not swallowing does to a body.
puzzles.why: Immobility and not drinking bring kidney injury, blood clots, pressure sores and aspiration. Catatonia can be fatal for these medical reasons, so the nursing and medical plan matters as much as the psychiatry.
puzzles.unlock: The consultant says: 'Let's do a lorazepam challenge.'

tags.objective: Risk: She hasn't moved, eaten or drunk for days.

puzzles.prompt: Put the lorazepam challenge in order.
items: Rate her catatonic signs at the start
Give a small dose of lorazepam
Re-rate the signs after a short wait
If better, give lorazepam regularly; if not, plan ECT
puzzles.hint: You can't measure a change without a starting point.
puzzles.why: A baseline rating, a test dose, then a repeat rating shows whether she responds. Most people with catatonia improve with benzodiazepines. ECT works well when they don't, and is urgent in malignant catatonia.
puzzles.unlock: After the dose she sits up and takes a sip of water.

tags.objective: Plan: Put the lorazepam challenge in order.

puzzles.prompt: The team plans her depression treatment. Which medicine stays off the chart for now?
options: An antidepressant once she can swallow
puzzles.why: After neuroleptic malignant syndrome, antipsychotics are avoided until it has fully settled, and restarted only with great care if needed. Lorazepam treats the catatonia; an antidepressant (or ECT) treats the depression.

tags.objective: Medicine: The team plans her depression treatment.

puzzles.prompt: To call it catatonia, at least how many of the 12 listed catatonic features must dominate the picture?
puzzles.hint: Fewer than she had on arrival.
puzzles.why: Three or more of the twelve (stupor, catalepsy, waxy flexibility, mutism, negativism, posturing, mannerism, stereotypy, agitation, grimacing, echolalia, echopraxia). She had four.

tags.objective: Criteria: To call it catatonia, at least how many of the 12 listed catatonic features must.

clues: Meera, 34, a school teacher, says she has 'no energy for anything' and has taken leave from work.
It started about six weeks ago. She can't name a trigger.
She has stopped enjoying her daughter's dance recitals and her evening walks.
She wakes at 4 a.m. and can't fall back asleep. She has lost 4 kg without trying.
She feels she is 'a burden on everyone' and finds it hard to correct even a page of homework.
She has never had a spell of feeling unusually high, wired or needing little sleep.

investigations.label: Mood and affect
investigations.result: Says 'empty'. Affect sad and constricted, slowed speech, no psychotic features.

investigations.label: Ask her husband
investigations.result: She cries most evenings and hardly eats. Before this she was lively. No spending sprees or sleepless high periods ever.

investigations.label: Blood tests
investigations.result: Thyroid function, blood count and B12 are normal.

differentials.whyNot: There is no clear stressor, and she meets full major depressive episode criteria (5+ symptoms for 2+ weeks).
Persistent depressive disorder needs low mood for at least 2 years. This is six weeks.
Bipolar II needs a past hypomanic episode (4+ days). Her husband confirms there has never been one.
Thyroid, blood count and B12 are normal, so there's no medical cause shown.

DAILY.pointer: Count the symptoms and check how long they have lasted.
DAILY.overview: A major depressive episode needs five or more symptoms for at least 2 weeks, one of them low mood or loss of interest. Meera has low mood, loss of pleasure, early waking, weight loss, worthlessness and poor concentration for six weeks. Always ask about past highs: one hypomanic episode changes the diagnosis to bipolar II. Check thyroid and B12 before settling on a primary depression.
refs: DSM-5-TR p.183 (MDD criteria A to E)
DAILY.objective: Count symptoms and duration to confirm a major depressive episode, and screen for past highs.

clues: Rohit, 41, an accountant, comes in because his wife said 'you are never happy'.
He says 'I've always been like this, it's just my nature'.
He feels low on more days than not, and has felt this way since his early thirties.
He sleeps too much on weekends, feels tired, and has little confidence at work.
In all these years he has never had two months in a row of feeling well.
He has never had a spell of five or more depressive symptoms together, and never a high.

investigations.label: Mood and affect
investigations.result: Mood 'so-so, like always'. Affect mildly restricted. Thinks clearly. No suicidal ideas.

investigations.label: Ask his wife
investigations.result: 'He's been gloomy for as long as I've known him, eight or nine years.' Works every day, never takes sick leave.

investigations.label: A rating scale
investigations.result: PHQ-9 score 9 (mild). Has stayed between 8 and 11 on three visits.

investigations.label: Blood tests
investigations.result: Thyroid function and blood count normal.

differentials.whyNot: He has never had 5 symptoms together. The picture is milder and lasts years, not weeks.
Cyclothymia needs repeated hypomanic-type spells too. He has never had a high.
There's no stressor, and it has lasted years, far beyond 6 months.

DAILY.pointer: Look at the time scale: weeks, months or years?
DAILY.overview: Persistent depressive disorder is low mood on more days than not for at least 2 years (1 year in children), with two or more symptoms such as poor sleep or appetite, low energy, low self-esteem, poor concentration or hopelessness, and no two-month break. People often call it their personality. It can coexist with major depressive episodes, which are then specified.
refs: DSM-5-TR p.193 (PDD criteria A to C)
DAILY.objective: Use the 2-year rule to tell persistent depressive disorder from a major depressive episode.

clues: Arjun, 23, a final-year student, is brought in by his parents at 2 a.m.
For ten days he has slept two or three hours a night and says he feels 'better than ever'.
He has spent ₹2 lakh on a business idea and wants to call the Prime Minister about it.
He talks fast and jumps from topic to topic; it is hard to get a word in.
He became angry and broke a window when his father took his debit card.
He has taken no drugs or medicines. Two years ago he had a long low spell.

investigations.label: Speech and thought
investigations.result: Pressured speech, flight of ideas, grandiose ideas of being destined to change the country. Insight absent.

investigations.label: Ask his parents
investigations.result: Normally a quiet boy. This came on over a few days. His uncle had 'the same illness' and takes lithium.

differentials.whyNot: This is a full manic episode: over a week, severe enough to break things and need admission. Bipolar II never has mania.
Drug screen negative and no drug history. Symptoms are mood-driven, not only delusions.
There's no period of psychosis without a mood episode.

DAILY.pointer: How many days, and how much harm? That decides mania versus hypomania.
DAILY.overview: A manic episode is at least 1 week (or any length if admission is needed) of raised or irritable mood plus raised energy, with three or more symptoms (four if only irritable): grandiosity, little need for sleep, pressured speech, racing thoughts, distractibility, more goal-directed activity, risky spending. One manic episode is enough for bipolar I. Family history and a prior depression make it more likely.
refs: DSM-5-TR p.150 (bipolar II has never had mania)
DAILY.objective: Recognise a manic episode and know one is enough for bipolar I.
