PREP.subject: statistics
PREP.stem: What is the mean of the scores 4, 8, 6, 10 and 12?
PREP.explanation: Step 1: add the scores: 4 + 8 + 6 + 10 + 12 = 40. Step 2: divide by the number of scores, N = 5: 40/5 = 8. So the mean is 8. 10 is the mean of only the three largest scores (8, 10, 12). 6 is one of the scores. 9 does not come from any standard calculation on these data.

PREP.subject: statistics
PREP.stem: What is the median of the scores 3, 7, 9, 12, 15 and 20?
PREP.explanation: With an even number of scores (N = 6) arranged in order, the median is the mean of the two middle scores (the 3rd and 4th): (9 + 12)/2 = 10.5. 9 and 12 are each only one of the two middle values. 11 is the mean of all six scores (66/6), not the median.

PREP.subject: statistics
PREP.stem: Which measure of central tendency is the only one appropriate for nominal data such as religion or blood group?
PREP.explanation: Nominal categories have no order or magnitude, so only the most frequent category (the mode) is meaningful. The median needs at least ordinal data, because the scores must be ranked. The mean and geometric mean need interval or ratio data.

PREP.subject: statistics
PREP.stem: Monthly household incomes in a city are strongly positively skewed. The usual order of the three averages is:
PREP.explanation: A long right tail of a few very high incomes pulls the mean upwards, the median lies in between, and the mode is at the peak, so mean > median > mode. 'Mode > median > mean' is the pattern for negative skew. Equality holds for a symmetrical unimodal distribution. The median falls between the other two, not above the mean.

PREP.subject: statistics
PREP.stem: Which of the following statistics are resistant (robust) to a few extreme outliers?
statements: Median
Mean
Interquartile range
Range
PREP.explanation: The median and IQR depend only on the middle of the ordered data, so a few extreme values barely change them. The mean is pulled towards outliers. The range is defined by the two most extreme values, so it is the least resistant measure of all.

PREP.subject: statistics
PREP.stem: Patients' pain is rated as none, mild, moderate or severe. The most appropriate measure of central tendency is the:
PREP.explanation: Pain categories are ordered, but the distances between them are unknown, which makes them ordinal. The median, the middle rank, is the best measure (the mode is also allowed). The mean needs equal intervals. The geometric and harmonic means need ratio data.

PREP.subject: statistics
PREP.stem: A distribution of exam scores has two clear peaks, one at 40 and one at 75. It is best described as:
PREP.explanation: Two distinct peaks make a bimodal distribution. It often suggests two subgroups, such as students who did and did not prepare. Skewness describes asymmetry with a single long tail. Leptokurtosis describes a single sharp peak with heavy tails. A rectangular (uniform) distribution has no peaks at all.

PREP.subject: statistics
PREP.stem: On an IQ test with mean 100 and SD 15, what is the z-score for an IQ of 130?
PREP.explanation: Step 1: z = (X − M)/SD. Step 2: X − M = 130 − 100 = 30. Step 3: 30/15 = 2.00. So an IQ of 130 lies 2 SDs above the mean, at about the 98th percentile. 1.30 divides X by 100 instead of finding the deviation. 1.50 divides 30 by 20. 3.00 divides 30 by 10.

data.caption: Every standard score is the same normal curve with a new ruler: z has mean 0 and SD 1, T mean 50 and SD 10, IQ mean 100 and SD 15, Wechsler subtests mean 10 and SD 3. One SD above the mean is about the 84th percentile on all of them.

PREP.subject: statistics
PREP.stem: In a normal distribution, approximately what percentage of scores lies between z = −1 and z = +1?
PREP.explanation: The normal table gives an area of .3413 between the mean and z = +1. The curve is symmetrical, so the area between the mean and z = −1 is also .3413. Adding them: .3413 + .3413 = .6826, about 68.26%. 34.13% is only one side of the mean. 95.44% is the area within ±2 SD, and 99.72% within ±3 SD.

data.caption: Every standard score is the same normal curve with a new ruler: z has mean 0 and SD 1, T mean 50 and SD 10, IQ mean 100 and SD 15, Wechsler subtests mean 10 and SD 3. One SD above the mean is about the 84th percentile on all of them.

PREP.subject: statistics
PREP.stem: A z-score of −1.2 is converted to a T-score (mean 50, SD 10). The T-score is:
PREP.explanation: Step 1: T-scores have mean 50 and SD 10, so T = 50 + 10z. Step 2: 10 × (−1.2) = −12. Step 3: T = 50 − 12 = 38. The score is 1.2 SDs below the mean on either scale. 62 ignores the minus sign. 48.8 adds z to 50 without multiplying by 10. 12 forgets to add the mean.

data.caption: Every standard score is the same normal curve with a new ruler: z has mean 0 and SD 1, T mean 50 and SD 10, IQ mean 100 and SD 15, Wechsler subtests mean 10 and SD 3. One SD above the mean is about the 84th percentile on all of them.

PREP.subject: statistics
PREP.stem: Two fair coins are tossed. What is the probability that both show heads?
PREP.explanation: The tosses are independent, so P(H and H) = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. There are four equally likely outcomes (HH, HT, TH, TT), and one of them is HH. 1/2 is the probability of heads on one coin. 1/3 wrongly treats 'two heads, one head, no heads' as equally likely. 1/8 is the probability for three coins.

PREP.subject: statistics
PREP.stem: Which of the following statements about probability are correct?
statements: A probability always lies between 0 and 1, inclusive.
The probabilities of all mutually exclusive and exhaustive outcomes add up to 1.
P(not A) = 1 − P(A).
A probability of 1.2 indicates a very likely event.
PREP.explanation: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are basic axioms and rules of probability: bounds, total probability and the complement rule. Statement 4 is impossible, because no probability can exceed 1. '1 and 2 only' and '1 and 3 only' each leave out a true rule.

PREP.subject: statistics
PREP.stem: A researcher concludes that a new therapy works when, in reality, it has no effect. This is a:
PREP.explanation: Rejecting a true null hypothesis (no effect) is a Type I error, a false positive, with probability α. A Type II error would be missing a real effect. The decision is wrong, so it is not correct. A sampling frame error concerns how a sample was drawn, not a decision about a hypothesis.

PREP.subject: statistics
PREP.stem: The probability of making a Type II error is denoted by:
PREP.explanation: β (beta) is the probability of a Type II error: failing to reject the null hypothesis when it is actually false, that is, missing a real effect. α is the probability of a Type I error (a false positive). 1 − α is the probability of correctly keeping a true null. 1 − β is power, the probability of correctly detecting a real effect.

PREP.subject: statistics
PREP.stem: A study is designed with α = .05 and β = .20. What is its statistical power?
PREP.explanation: Power is the probability of detecting an effect that is really there, which is 1 minus the probability of missing it: power = 1 − β = 1 − .20 = .80. This is the conventional minimum Cohen recommended. .95 is 1 − α, the probability of correctly keeping a true null. .05 and .20 are the two error probabilities themselves.

PREP.subject: statistics
PREP.stem: Which correlation coefficient shows the strongest linear relationship?
PREP.explanation: The strength of a correlation is judged by its size ignoring the sign, |r|. The sign only shows direction: positive (both rise together) or negative (one rises as the other falls). |−.85| = .85 is the largest value here, so it is the strongest relationship. +.60 and −.40 are moderate, and +.05 is close to zero.

PREP.subject: statistics
PREP.stem: Study hours and exam marks correlate r = .70. What percentage of the variance in marks is shared with (accounted for by) study hours?
PREP.explanation: Step 1: the proportion of shared variance is the coefficient of determination, r². Step 2: .70² = .70 × .70 = .49. Step 3: as a percentage, 49%. So about half the variation in marks goes with variation in study hours, and about 51% is due to other factors. 70% wrongly treats r as a proportion of variance. 84% is √.70. 7% misplaces the decimal point.

PREP.subject: statistics
PREP.stem: Children's shoe size correlates strongly with their reading ability. Which statements are correct?
statements: Correlation alone does not show that bigger feet cause better reading.
A third variable, age, plausibly explains the association.
The correlation must be a calculation error.
Controlling for age would be expected to reduce the correlation greatly.
PREP.explanation: Older children have larger feet and read better, so age drives both (1 and 2). A partial correlation controlling for age would be expected to drop to near zero (4). Statement 3 is false: the correlation is real; it is the causal reading of it that is wrong.

PREP.subject: statistics
PREP.stem: In a scatterplot, points run from the upper left to the lower right in a fairly narrow band. This indicates:
PREP.explanation: Down-sloping points mean that higher X goes with lower Y (negative), and a narrow band means a strong relationship. A positive correlation slopes upwards. No correlation shows a shapeless cloud. A curvilinear relationship shows a bend in the pattern.

PREP.subject: statistics
PREP.stem: In the regression equation Ŷ = a + bX, the coefficient b represents:
options: The predicted value of Y when X is zero
The correlation between X and Y
The predicted change in Y for a one-unit increase in X
PREP.explanation: b is the slope: the change in Ŷ for each one-unit increase in X. The predicted Y when X = 0 is the intercept, a. b equals r only when both variables are standardised. The standard error of estimate measures the spread of the residuals.

PREP.subject: statistics
PREP.stem: In regression, a residual is:
options: The slope of the regression line, showing the change in Y for each unit of X
The difference between an observed Y and the Y predicted by the equation
The correlation between two predictors in the same equation
The value of X at which the predicted Y equals zero
PREP.explanation: Residual = Y − Ŷ, the prediction error for each case. Least squares minimises the sum of squared residuals. The slope is b. The correlation between predictors relates to multicollinearity. The X value when Y is zero is the x-intercept, which is rarely of interest.

PREP.subject: statistics
PREP.stem: The 'least-squares' regression line is the line that:
options: Minimises the sum of the absolute values of X across all the cases
Passes through the largest possible number of the observed data points in the plot
Minimises the sum of squared differences between observed and predicted Y
Maximises the correlation between X and Y
PREP.explanation: Ordinary least squares picks a and b to minimise Σ(Y − Ŷ)². A line through the most points is not a statistical criterion. Minimising the sum of |X| is meaningless. The correlation is a fixed property of the data, which no choice of line can change.

PREP.subject: statistics
PREP.stem: The regression equation for exam marks is Ŷ = 30 + 2.5X, where X is hours of revision. What does 2.5 mean?
options: A student who does no revision is predicted to score 2.5
Each extra hour of revision is associated with 2.5 more predicted marks
PREP.explanation: 2.5 is the slope, the predicted increase in marks per hour. The predicted score with zero hours is the intercept, 30. The slope is not r, which would need the SDs to compute. Variance explained is R², which cannot be read from b alone.

PREP.subject: statistics
PREP.stem: A counsellor wants to know whether her 25 clients' mean wellbeing score differs from the published population mean of 50. The population SD is not known. Which test fits?
PREP.explanation: One sample is being compared with a known population value, and σ has to be estimated from the sample, so the one-sample t-test is right. An independent-samples t-test compares two separate groups. A paired t-test compares two scores from the same people. Chi-square goodness of fit compares observed category frequencies with expected ones, not a mean.

PREP.subject: cognitive
PREP.stem: In Atkinson and Shiffrin's multi-store model, information passes through which sequence of stores?
options: Long-term store → short-term store → sensory register
Episodic buffer → phonological loop → central executive
Sensory register → short-term store → long-term store
Iconic store → procedural store → semantic store
PREP.explanation: The modal model proposes a sensory register, a limited short-term store, and a durable long-term store, with control processes such as rehearsal moving information along. Long-term to short-term to sensory reverses the flow. The episodic buffer, phonological loop and central executive are parts of Baddeley's working memory model. The iconic, procedural and semantic sequence mixes sensory, procedural and semantic memory, which are not stages of this model.

data.caption: In the multi-store model information enters a large but brief sensory register, attention moves some into short-term memory (about 7 items for about 20 seconds), and rehearsal moves it into long-term memory, from which it is retrieved back into short-term memory for use.

PREP.subject: cognitive
PREP.stem: George Miller's 'magical number seven, plus or minus two' refers to
options: the capacity of short-term memory, measured in chunks
the number of seconds information lasts in iconic memory
the number of stages in memory processing
the number of items in long-term memory
PREP.explanation: Miller argued that immediate memory span is limited to about 7 ± 2 chunks, meaningful units that can be enlarged by recoding. Iconic memory lasts well under a second. Memory models do not have seven stages. Long-term memory has no known capacity limit.

PREP.subject: cognitive
PREP.stem: Cowan argued that when rehearsal and chunking are prevented, the true capacity of short-term (focus of attention) memory is about
PREP.explanation: Cowan's review suggested that Miller's 7 ± 2 was inflated by rehearsal and grouping; pure capacity is about 3 to 5 chunks. 7 ± 2 is Miller's estimate. 15 to 20 items exceeds any estimate of STM. One item is the estimate of some theorists for the narrow focus of attention itself, not general STM capacity.

PREP.subject: cognitive
PREP.stem: Sperling's partial-report experiments showed that iconic memory
options: lasts several minutes if the display is brief
holds more than can be reported, but decays within about a second
holds only about four items at any moment
stores information in a semantic, meaning-based code
PREP.explanation: When a tone cued one row immediately after a brief display, people reported most of that row, implying that most of the display was briefly available; with a 1-second delay the advantage vanished. It does not last minutes. The four-item limit was the whole-report limit, caused by decay during reporting. The icon is a raw visual (pre-categorical) store, not semantic.

data.caption: In the multi-store model information enters a large but brief sensory register, attention moves some into short-term memory (about 7 items for about 20 seconds), and rehearsal moves it into long-term memory, from which it is retrieved back into short-term memory for use.

PREP.subject: cognitive
PREP.stem: A display of 3 rows × 4 letters is flashed for 50 ms. When a tone immediately cues one row, participants report on average 3 of the 4 letters in that row. Using Sperling's logic, about how many letters were available in iconic memory?
PREP.explanation: Because the row is chosen at random after the display, the proportion reported from the cued row (3/4 = 75%) estimates the proportion of the whole display available: .75 × 12 = 9 letters. 3 is the raw row score. 4.5 is the typical whole-report score, limited by decay during report. 12 assumes perfect availability.

data.caption: In the multi-store model information enters a large but brief sensory register, attention moves some into short-term memory (about 7 items for about 20 seconds), and rehearsal moves it into long-term memory, from which it is retrieved back into short-term memory for use.

PREP.subject: cognitive
PREP.stem: Darwin, Turvey and Crowder's 'three-eared man' study, in which letters were presented from the left, right and centre at once, provided evidence for
options: an auditory sensory (echoic) store lasting about 2 seconds or more
a visual store lasting about 250 ms after the display
the phonological similarity effect in short-term memory
late selection of attention among three channels
PREP.explanation: Using an auditory version of partial report, they found a partial-report advantage that declined over about 2 to 4 seconds, longer than the icon. The 250 ms store is iconic memory. Phonological similarity concerns short-term memory confusions. The study was about sensory memory, not attentional selection.

PREP.subject: cognitive
PREP.stem: In the Brown-Peterson task, participants hear a consonant trigram and then count backwards by threes before recall. The main finding was that
options: recall stayed near 100% for a minute
recall was better after longer delays
recall fell sharply, to about 10% after 18 seconds
PREP.explanation: Peterson and Peterson found rapid forgetting when rehearsal was blocked, which they attributed to decay. Recall did not stay perfect, counting did not help (it prevented rehearsal), and longer delays produced worse, not better, recall.

PREP.subject: cognitive
PREP.stem: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) and choose the correct option.
statements: Keppel and Underwood found heavy forgetting on the first trial of the Brown-Peterson task, as rapid decay would predict.
Much of the forgetting in the Brown-Peterson task reflects proactive interference from items on earlier trials.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
PREP.explanation: A is false, R is true. Keppel and Underwood found almost no forgetting on trial 1, even after long delays, because there are no earlier trigrams to interfere. Forgetting builds up over trials as proactive interference accumulates, which is what R states. This challenged the original decay interpretation of Peterson and Peterson.

data.title: Forgetting, and how to slow it
data.caption: Watch the curve fall steeply in the first hours, then level off (Ebbinghaus, testing himself with nonsense syllables and measuring savings on relearning). Add spaced reviews: each one lifts memory and makes the next fall slower. Some forgetting is decay, but much is interference: old learning blocks new (proactive), new learning blocks old (retroactive).

PREP.subject: cognitive
PREP.stem: In Wickens' 'release from proactive interference', recall in the Brown-Peterson task recovers when
options: the retention interval is lengthened, giving the earlier items time to fade away
the category of the items is changed, for example from fruits to professions
participants are allowed to rehearse during the interval
the same items are repeated on every trial
PREP.explanation: Proactive interference builds up when successive items share a category; switching to a new category releases it, showing that short-term memory items are coded by meaning as well as sound. A longer interval increases forgetting. Allowing rehearsal changes the task rather than releasing PI. Repetition increases, not reduces, similarity.

data.title: Forgetting, and how to slow it
data.caption: Watch the curve fall steeply in the first hours, then level off (Ebbinghaus, testing himself with nonsense syllables and measuring savings on relearning). Add spaced reviews: each one lifts memory and makes the next fall slower. Some forgetting is decay, but much is interference: old learning blocks new (proactive), new learning blocks old (retroactive).

PREP.subject: cognitive
PREP.stem: In Waugh and Norman's probe-digit task, digits were presented at either 1 or 4 per second. Forgetting depended on the number of digits that followed the probe, not on the elapsed time. This supports
options: trace decay over time as the main cause of short-term forgetting
a separate echoic store for the spoken digits
interference rather than decay as the main cause of short-term forgetting
PREP.explanation: If decay were the cause, faster presentation (less elapsed time) should reduce forgetting for the same number of intervening items; it did not. Forgetting tracked the number of interfering items. The study does not concern echoic memory or depth of processing.

data.title: Forgetting, and how to slow it
data.caption: Watch the curve fall steeply in the first hours, then level off (Ebbinghaus, testing himself with nonsense syllables and measuring savings on relearning). Add spaced reviews: each one lifts memory and makes the next fall slower. Some forgetting is decay, but much is interference: old learning blocks new (proactive), new learning blocks old (retroactive).

PREP.subject: cognitive
PREP.stem: In the serial position curve for free recall, the recency effect is usually explained by
options: the last items still being held in short-term memory at the time of recall
the last items having been rehearsed most
the last items being transferred to long-term memory first
PREP.explanation: Recency reflects output from short-term memory, which is why a filled delay removes it. Extra rehearsal explains primacy, not recency; early items get rehearsed most. Recent items have had the least chance to reach long-term memory. Proactive interference would impair, not enhance, recall.

data.caption: In free recall the first words (primacy, rehearsed into long-term memory) and the last words (recency, still in short-term memory) are remembered best. A 30-second distracting delay removes recency but leaves primacy.

PREP.subject: cognitive
PREP.stem: Which statements correctly describe Glanzer and Cunitz's serial-position findings?
statements: A 30-second filled delay before recall removed the recency effect.
The filled delay left the primacy effect largely intact.
Slower presentation improved recall of early and middle items.
Slower presentation selectively enhanced the recency effect.
PREP.explanation: Statements 1 to 3 are their findings: delay affected only the end of the curve, while slower presentation (more rehearsal time) affected only earlier positions. This double dissociation supports separate short- and long-term components. Statement 4 is false: recency was unaffected by presentation rate.

data.caption: In free recall the first words (primacy, rehearsed into long-term memory) and the last words (recency, still in short-term memory) are remembered best. A 30-second distracting delay removes recency but leaves primacy.

PREP.subject: cognitive
PREP.stem: Match the experimental paradigm (List I) with the researchers associated with it (List II).

left: Delayed free recall and the serial position curve
Partial report of a letter array

PREP.explanation: Serial position with delay = Glanzer and Cunitz (A-III); partial report = Sperling (B-IV); probe digit = Waugh and Norman (C-I); three-eared man = Darwin, Turvey and Crowder (D-II). A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II swaps Glanzer-Cunitz and Sperling. A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II swaps Sperling and Waugh-Norman. A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I swaps the last two.

data.caption: In free recall the first words (primacy, rehearsed into long-term memory) and the last words (recency, still in short-term memory) are remembered best. A 30-second distracting delay removes recency but leaves primacy.

PREP.subject: cognitive
PREP.stem: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) and choose the correct option.
statements: Patient KF had a digit span of about two items yet could learn new long-term information fairly normally.
In the Atkinson-Shiffrin model, information must pass through the short-term store to enter the long-term store.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
PREP.explanation: Both statements are true, but R does not explain A; in fact KF's case, described by Shallice and Warrington, challenges R. If STS were the only gateway to LTS, a severe STS deficit should impair new long-term learning. KF's preserved learning suggested parallel routes or a non-unitary short-term memory, one motivation for the working memory model.

data.title: Follow a memory through the system
data.caption: Play it. Sensory memory holds a lot for under a second (iconic) or a few seconds (echoic); attention moves a little into short-term or working memory, which holds about 4 chunks (Miller said 7 plus or minus 2) for about 20 seconds without rehearsal; deeper, meaningful encoding moves it into long-term memory, and retrieval works best when the cues at test match those at learning.

PREP.subject: cognitive
PREP.stem: After bilateral medial temporal lobe surgery in 1953, patient H.M. showed
options: loss of all short-term memory, including digit span
inability to learn any new motor skills such as mirror drawing
loss of intelligence and language along with memory
severe anterograde amnesia, with normal digit span and intact skill learning
PREP.explanation: Scoville and Milner described H.M.'s profound anterograde amnesia for new facts and events, with intact short-term memory, intelligence and language; he improved at mirror drawing across days without remembering the practice. His digit span was normal, so short-term memory was not lost. He learned mirror drawing, so motor skill learning was intact. His intelligence and language were preserved.

data.title: The memory circuit

notes.hippocampus: Hippocampus (medial temporal lobe): turns new experiences into lasting conscious memories. H.M. lost it on both sides and could form almost no new facts or events, though old memories, short-term memory and new skills survived.
notes.thalamus: The mammillary bodies and the medial dorsal thalamus are damaged in Korsakoff syndrome (thiamine deficiency): severe new-learning loss with confabulation.
notes.amygdala: Amygdala: adds emotional strength, so frightening events are remembered better.
notes.prefrontal: Prefrontal cortex: working memory, strategy and remembering where a memory came from.
notes.basal-ganglia: Basal ganglia and cerebellum: skills and habits, which is why H.M. could still learn mirror drawing.

data.caption: Tap each part. The hippocampus forms new conscious memories; skills depend on other systems.

PREP.subject: cognitive
PREP.stem: Baddeley and Hitch's original working memory model had three components. Which set is correct?
options: Sensory register, short-term store, long-term store
Central executive, phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad
PREP.explanation: The 1974 model had a central executive controlling two slave systems, the phonological loop and visuospatial sketchpad; the episodic buffer was added in 2000. Sensory register, short-term store and long-term store is the Atkinson-Shiffrin model. Episodic, semantic and procedural are long-term memory systems. Iconic, echoic and haptic are sensory stores.

data.caption: Baddeley's working memory has a central executive directing two slave systems, the phonological loop for sounds and words and the visuospatial sketchpad for images, plus the episodic buffer that binds them and links to long-term memory.

PREP.subject: cognitive
PREP.stem: In 2000, Baddeley added a fourth component to the working memory model, which integrates information from the subsystems and long-term memory into multimodal episodes. It is the
PREP.explanation: The episodic buffer is a limited-capacity store that binds information from different sources into coherent episodes. The articulatory control process is part of the phonological loop. The inner scribe is part of the visuospatial sketchpad (Logie). The supervisory attentional system is Norman and Shallice's model, used to describe the central executive.

data.caption: Baddeley's working memory has a central executive directing two slave systems, the phonological loop for sounds and words and the visuospatial sketchpad for images, plus the episodic buffer that binds them and links to long-term memory.

PREP.subject: cognitive
PREP.stem: The phonological loop consists of
options: a phonological store and an articulatory rehearsal (control) process
a visual cache and an inner scribe for spatial information
a central executive and an episodic buffer that links the other stores
PREP.explanation: The phonological store holds speech-based traces for about 2 seconds; the articulatory process refreshes them by subvocal rehearsal and recodes visual material into phonological form. The visual cache and inner scribe make up the visuospatial sketchpad. The executive and buffer are separate components. Iconic and echoic are sensory memories.

data.caption: Baddeley's working memory has a central executive directing two slave systems, the phonological loop for sounds and words and the visuospatial sketchpad for images, plus the episodic buffer that binds them and links to long-term memory.

PREP.subject: cognitive
PREP.stem: The word-length effect in immediate serial recall shows that
options: long words are recalled better, because their extra syllables make them more distinctive and memorable
word length affects only long-term memory, not immediate recall
span depends on the number of syllables in the first word
span is smaller for words that take longer to say, about what can be said in 2 seconds
PREP.explanation: Baddeley, Thomson and Buchanan found span was lower for long words and closely matched reading rate, implying a time-limited rehearsal loop. Long words are recalled worse, not better. The effect is in immediate (short-term) recall. It depends on total articulation time, not the first word.

data.title: Working memory in action
data.caption: Play it and stop at working memory. In Baddeley's model it has a central executive (attention control, no storage), a phonological loop (inner voice and ear: articulatory suppression and the word-length effect hit it), a visuospatial sketchpad, and, added in 2000, an episodic buffer that binds information and links to long-term memory. Two tasks clash only when they need the same part.

PREP.subject: cognitive
PREP.stem: Conrad found that people recalling visually presented letter lists confused letters such as B, D, G and P. This phonological similarity effect indicates that
options: short-term memory uses only visual codes, so similar shapes are confused
visual items are recoded into a sound-based form in short-term memory
long-term memory is acoustic rather than semantic
attention fails when letters have similar shapes
PREP.explanation: Even with visual presentation, errors were acoustic, so letters had been recoded into speech-based form in short-term memory. If STM used only visual codes, confusions would follow letter shapes (E and F) instead. LTM tends to be semantic, as Baddeley showed. Attention to shapes is unrelated to sound-based confusions.

data.title: Follow a memory through the system
data.caption: Play it. Sensory memory holds a lot for under a second (iconic) or a few seconds (echoic); attention moves a little into short-term or working memory, which holds about 4 chunks (Miller said 7 plus or minus 2) for about 20 seconds without rehearsal; deeper, meaningful encoding moves it into long-term memory, and retrieval works best when the cues at test match those at learning.

PREP.subject: cognitive
PREP.stem: Which statements about articulatory suppression (repeating 'the, the, the' during a memory task) are correct?
statements: It abolishes the word-length effect for both visual and auditory presentation.
It abolishes the phonological similarity effect when items are presented visually.
It does not abolish the phonological similarity effect when items are presented auditorily.
It improves immediate serial recall by freeing the central executive.
PREP.explanation: Suppression blocks rehearsal (removing the word-length effect whatever the modality) and blocks recoding of visual items into the phonological store (removing the similarity effect for visual lists). Spoken items enter the store directly, so similarity effects remain for auditory lists. Statement 4 is false: suppression lowers span.

data.title: Working memory in action
data.caption: Play it and stop at working memory. In Baddeley's model it has a central executive (attention control, no storage), a phonological loop (inner voice and ear: articulatory suppression and the word-length effect hit it), a visuospatial sketchpad, and, added in 2000, an episodic buffer that binds information and links to long-term memory. Two tasks clash only when they need the same part.

PREP.subject: cognitive
PREP.stem: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) and choose the correct option.
statements: Under articulatory suppression, the phonological similarity effect remains for auditorily presented lists.
Spoken material gains obligatory, direct access to the phonological store without needing the articulatory control process.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
PREP.explanation: Both true; R explains A. The articulatory process is needed to get visual material into the store; suppression occupies it. Spoken words enter the store automatically, so their phonological similarity still causes confusions. This modality asymmetry is a key piece of evidence for the two-part phonological loop.

data.caption: Baddeley's working memory has a central executive directing two slave systems, the phonological loop for sounds and words and the visuospatial sketchpad for images, plus the episodic buffer that binds them and links to long-term memory.

PREP.subject: cognitive
PREP.stem: The 'irrelevant speech effect' refers to the finding that
options: people cannot hear speech while they are reading silently
irrelevant speech improves serial recall by raising arousal and alertness
background speech impairs serial recall of visual items, even when people try to ignore it
irrelevant speech affects only spatial memory, not verbal
PREP.explanation: Salamé and Baddeley showed that background speech, even in an unknown language, disrupts serial recall, consistent with obligatory access of speech to the phonological store. People can hear speech while reading. Speech impairs rather than improves recall. Spatial memory is affected little.

PREP.subject: cognitive
PREP.stem: Logie divided the visuospatial sketchpad into
options: a visual cache for form and colour and an inner scribe for spatial information
a phonological store and an articulatory rehearsal process
an episodic buffer and a semantic buffer linked to long-term memory
a dorsal and a ventral attention network for orienting
PREP.explanation: Logie proposed a passive visual cache and an active inner scribe, analogous to the store and rehearsal process of the phonological loop. The phonological store and articulatory process belong to the loop. 'Episodic and semantic buffer' is invented. Dorsal and ventral networks describe attention, not the sketchpad.

data.caption: Baddeley's working memory has a central executive directing two slave systems, the phonological loop for sounds and words and the visuospatial sketchpad for images, plus the episodic buffer that binds them and links to long-term memory.

PREP.subject: biological
PREP.stem: The resting membrane potential of a typical mammalian neuron is closest to:
PREP.explanation: A typical neuron rests at about -70 mV (range roughly -60 to -80 mV), inside negative relative to outside. +40 mV is near the peak of the action potential (overshoot), not rest. -20 mV is a depolarised value well past the usual threshold (about -55 mV). 0 mV would mean no potential difference across the membrane, which happens only if the ion gradients are lost.
PREP.ref: Kalat, Biological Psychology, ch. 2; Pinel, Biopsychology, ch. 4

PREP.subject: biological
PREP.stem: For each cycle that uses one ATP, the sodium-potassium pump moves:
PREP.explanation: The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase exports 3 Na⁺ and imports 2 K⁺ per ATP, which keeps Na⁺ high outside and K⁺ high inside and makes the pump slightly electrogenic (net one positive charge out). '2 out, 3 in' reverses the numbers. '3 Na⁺ in, 2 K⁺ out' reverses the directions, which would run the gradients down. A 1:1 exchange would be electroneutral, which the pump is not.

PREP.subject: biological
PREP.stem: The 'all-or-none law' states that:
options: A neuron releases all of its transmitter vesicles or none of them with each spike
All neurons fire at the same time or none fire
Once threshold is reached, the action potential has a fixed size whatever the stimulus strength
Postsynaptic potentials either reach the axon hillock at full size or else decay away completely
PREP.explanation: The action potential's amplitude does not grow with stimulus strength once threshold is crossed; stimulus intensity is coded instead by firing rate (rate law) and by the number of neurons recruited. Neurons do not fire in unison. Transmitter release is graded and quantal, not all-or-none. Postsynaptic potentials are graded and decay with distance; the law is about the spike, not PSPs.

PREP.subject: biological
PREP.stem: The part of the neuron that mainly receives incoming signals from other neurons is the:
PREP.explanation: Dendrites (with their spines) receive most synaptic input and pass graded potentials toward the soma. The axon carries the action potential away from the soma. Terminal buttons release transmitter to the next cell. Myelin insulates the axon; it is made by glia, not by the neuron itself.

data.caption: Signals come in at the dendrites, are summed at the cell body, and if they reach threshold at the axon hillock an action potential runs down the axon to the terminals, which release transmitter.

PREP.subject: biological
PREP.stem: Which part of a typical neuron receives most of the incoming signals from other neurons?
PREP.explanation: Dendrites are the branching extensions of the cell body. They are covered with receptors where other neurons' axon terminals form synapses, so they collect most incoming signals. Axon terminals are at the other end of the neuron; they release neurotransmitter onto the next cell, so they send signals rather than receive them. The myelin sheath is a fatty wrapping around the axon that speeds conduction; it receives nothing. The axon hillock is where incoming signals are summed and where the action potential usually starts, but the signals arrive mainly through the dendrites and cell body first.

data.caption: Signals come in at the dendrites, are summed at the cell body, and if they reach threshold at the axon hillock an action potential runs down the axon to the terminals, which release transmitter.

PREP.subject: biological
PREP.stem: The main job of the myelin sheath around many axons is to:
options: Speed up the conduction of action potentials along the axon
Produce neurotransmitters and carry them down to the synapse for release
Supply the neuron with blood and oxygen
PREP.explanation: Myelin is a fatty insulating layer made by oligodendrocytes in the brain and spinal cord and by Schwann cells in peripheral nerves. It forces the impulse to jump from one gap in the sheath (node of Ranvier) to the next, called saltatory conduction, which makes conduction much faster and saves energy. Neurotransmitters are made in the neuron itself, in the cell body or axon terminals, not in myelin. Receiving signals is mainly the job of dendrites. Blood supply comes through capillaries, and nutrients are passed on partly by astrocytes, not by myelin. Diseases that strip myelin, such as multiple sclerosis, slow or block conduction.

data.caption: Myelin is wrapped round the axon in layers, with gaps called nodes of Ranvier. The signal jumps from node to node, so it travels far faster. Schwann cells wrap one stretch of one nerve in the body; an oligodendrocyte wraps many axons in the brain and cord.

PREP.subject: biological
PREP.ref: Bear, Connors and Paradiso, action potential
PREP.stem: The rapid rising (depolarising) phase of the action potential is caused mainly by:
options: Calcium pumped out of the cell
PREP.explanation: When the membrane reaches threshold, voltage-gated sodium channels open and sodium rushes in down its concentration and electrical gradients, driving the membrane towards the sodium equilibrium potential. Potassium efflux through voltage-gated potassium channels causes repolarisation afterwards. Chloride entry hyperpolarises and underlies many inhibitory potentials. Calcium pumping maintains low internal calcium but does not drive the axonal spike.

PREP.subject: biological
PREP.stem: In the peripheral nervous system, myelin is formed by:
PREP.explanation: Schwann cells myelinate peripheral axons, each wrapping a single segment of one axon; in the brain and spinal cord oligodendrocytes form myelin, each myelinating segments of many axons. Astrocytes support synapses, regulate ions and contribute to the blood-brain barrier. Microglia are the resident immune cells. This difference matters clinically: multiple sclerosis targets central myelin, Guillain-Barre syndrome peripheral myelin.

data.caption: Myelin is wrapped round the axon in layers, with gaps called nodes of Ranvier. The signal jumps from node to node, so it travels far faster. Schwann cells wrap one stretch of one nerve in the body; an oligodendrocyte wraps many axons in the brain and cord.

PREP.subject: biological
PREP.ref: Bear, Connors and Paradiso, synaptic integration
PREP.stem: An excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP) is:
options: A brief hyperpolarisation of the postsynaptic membrane
An all-or-none spike travelling along the axon
A graded depolarisation that makes firing more likely
A permanent change in resting potential
PREP.explanation: An EPSP is a small, graded depolarisation of the postsynaptic membrane, usually from cation entry through glutamate receptors; it spreads passively and decays with distance and time, and many EPSPs summate to bring the axon hillock to threshold. Hyperpolarisation describes an inhibitory potential. The all-or-none spike is the action potential itself. EPSPs are transient, not permanent shifts.

PREP.subject: biological
PREP.stem: Which researchers worked out the ionic basis of the action potential using the squid giant axon and the voltage clamp?
PREP.explanation: Hodgkin and Huxley used the voltage clamp on the squid giant axon in the late 1940s and early 1950s to show that the action potential results from sequential sodium and potassium conductance changes, and modelled them mathematically; they shared the 1963 Nobel Prize. Hubel and Wiesel studied visual cortex. Bliss and Lomo described long-term potentiation. Neher and Sakmann developed the patch clamp for single channels.

PREP.subject: biological
PREP.stem: Action potentials normally travel in one direction along the axon, away from the cell body, because:
options: The membrane behind it is refractory
Myelin blocks any backward flow of current
Dendrites absorb all of the backward current
Sodium channels exist only at the axon terminal
PREP.explanation: Behind the active region, sodium channels are inactivated and potassium channels are still open, so that membrane is refractory and cannot fire again immediately; current therefore excites only the membrane ahead. Myelin speeds conduction but does not determine direction, and unmyelinated axons also conduct one way. Back-propagating spikes into dendrites do occur. Sodium channels are found along the axon, densely at the hillock and nodes.

data.caption: Signals come in at the dendrites, are summed at the cell body, and if they reach threshold at the axon hillock an action potential runs down the axon to the terminals, which release transmitter.

PREP.subject: biological
PREP.stem: The resting potential lies much closer to the equilibrium potential of K⁺ than to that of Na⁺ because, at rest, the membrane:
options: Is far more permeable to K⁺ than to Na⁺ through open leak channels
Actively pumps K⁺ out of the cell faster than Na⁺
Contains more voltage-gated K⁺ channels than voltage-gated Na⁺ channels
PREP.explanation: By the Goldman equation, membrane potential is a permeability-weighted average of the ion equilibrium potentials. At rest K⁺ leak channels make permeability to K⁺ roughly 25 to 40 times that to Na⁺, so the potential sits near E_K (about -90 mV). The pump moves K⁺ in, not out (3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in). The membrane is not completely impermeable to Na⁺: a small Na⁺ leak is why rest (-70 mV) is less negative than E_K. Voltage-gated channels are mostly closed at rest, so their number does not set the resting potential.
PREP.ref: Kandel, Principles of Neural Science, ch. 9 (Goldman equation)

PREP.subject: biological
PREP.stem: The absolute refractory period of an axon is mainly caused by:
options: Depletion of neurotransmitter from the terminal
Temporary failure of the Na⁺/K⁺ pump
PREP.explanation: After opening, voltage-gated Na⁺ channels enter an inactivated state (the inactivation 'h' gate closes) and cannot reopen until the membrane repolarises, so no stimulus, however strong, can fire a second spike. Open K⁺ channels and the after-hyperpolarisation account for the relative refractory period, when a stronger-than-usual stimulus can fire the cell. Transmitter depletion is a synaptic, not axonal, event. The pump works slowly and is not responsible for spike-by-spike recovery.

PREP.subject: biological
PREP.stem: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) and choose the correct option.
statements: Conduction velocity is faster in myelinated axons than in unmyelinated axons of the same diameter.
Myelin is formed by oligodendrocytes in the central nervous system and by Schwann cells in the peripheral nervous system.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
PREP.explanation: Both statements are true, but R does not explain A. A is true because myelin insulates the axon, so current spreads quickly and passively under each myelinated stretch and the slow step of regenerating the spike happens only at the nodes of Ranvier (saltatory conduction). R is also true, but it only says which cells make myelin; it says nothing about why myelin speeds conduction. In exams, check whether R gives the mechanism behind A, not just a related fact.

data.caption: Myelin is wrapped round the axon in layers, with gaps called nodes of Ranvier. The signal jumps from node to node, so it travels far faster. Schwann cells wrap one stretch of one nerve in the body; an oligodendrocyte wraps many axons in the brain and cord.

PREP.subject: biological
PREP.stem: Match the cell in List I with its main function in List II.

right: Myelinates a single segment of one peripheral axon
Immune defence and removal of debris in the CNS
Myelinates segments of several CNS axons
Buffers extracellular K⁺, supports the blood-brain barrier and takes up glutamate

PREP.explanation: Oligodendrocytes send processes to myelinate segments of many CNS axons (iii); a Schwann cell wraps one segment of one peripheral axon (i). Microglia are the CNS's resident immune cells (ii). Astrocytes buffer K⁺, clear glutamate and contribute to the blood-brain barrier (iv). The code A-I, B-III, C-II, D-IV swaps the two myelinating cells, a common confusion. The code A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II swaps the astrocyte and microglia roles, and A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III swaps the astrocyte and oligodendrocyte roles.

PREP.stem: In most neurons, the action potential is first generated at the:
PREP.explanation: The axon initial segment has the highest density of voltage-gated Na⁺ channels and so the lowest threshold; summed postsynaptic potentials reaching it decide whether the cell fires. Dendritic spines receive excitatory synapses and generate graded EPSPs (some dendrites can produce local spikes, but they are not the usual trigger zone). The soma integrates input but has a higher threshold. The presynaptic terminal is where the spike ends and triggers release.

PREP.subject: biological
PREP.stem: Which of the following statements about postsynaptic potentials are correct?
statements: EPSPs and IPSPs are graded potentials whose size varies with the amount of transmitter.
Spatial summation is the adding together of potentials arriving close together in time at a single synapse.
An IPSP can be produced by Cl⁻ entering the cell or by K⁺ leaving it.
PSPs decay as they spread passively along the membrane.
PREP.explanation: A is correct: PSPs are graded, not all-or-none. B is wrong: it describes temporal summation; spatial summation adds inputs from different synapses arriving at the same time. C is correct: GABA-A receptors let Cl⁻ in and GABA-B receptors open K⁺ channels, and both hyperpolarise or stabilise the membrane. D is correct: PSPs spread electrotonically and shrink with distance, which is why synapses near the soma have more influence. So 1, 3 and 4 only.

Multiple sclerosis: central oligodendrocyte myelin; Guillain-Barré: peripheral Schwann cell myelin
Both affect only the neuron's cell body, not myelin
PREP.explanation: Multiple sclerosis is an immune attack on CNS myelin made by oligodendrocytes, producing plaques in the brain and spinal cord. Guillain-Barré syndrome is an acute immune attack on peripheral nerves (Schwann cell myelin, sometimes axons), producing ascending weakness. The option giving multiple sclerosis peripheral myelin and Guillain-Barré central myelin reverses them. Neither is confined to central myelin, and both target myelin rather than the cell body.

PREP.stem: The arrival of an action potential at a presynaptic terminal triggers transmitter release mainly by:
options: Opening ligand-gated Na⁺ channels on the vesicles, letting Na⁺ in to trigger fusion
Opening voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels, letting Ca²⁺ in to trigger vesicle fusion
PREP.explanation: Depolarisation opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels (mainly N- and P/Q-type) at the active zone; Ca²⁺ binds synaptotagmin, and SNARE proteins fuse the vesicle with the membrane. Vesicles do not carry ligand-gated Na⁺ channels. Reuptake transporters clear transmitter after release. Closing K⁺ leak channels would depolarise the terminal but is not the trigger for release.

PREP.subject: biological
PREP.stem: Repolarisation of the action potential depends mainly on:
options: Opening of chloride channels along the axon
Closing of potassium leak channels at rest
K+ channel opening and Na+ channel inactivation
PREP.explanation: After the peak, voltage-gated sodium channels inactivate and delayed-rectifier potassium channels open, allowing potassium efflux that returns the membrane towards rest and briefly beyond (the after-hyperpolarisation). The sodium-potassium pump maintains gradients over the long term but is too slow to repolarise a single spike. Chloride channels are not the main repolarising current in axons. Closing leak channels would depolarise rather than repolarise.

PREP.subject: biological
PREP.ref: Bear, Connors and Paradiso, synaptic integration
PREP.stem: Two weak synapses at different places on a dendrite fire at the same moment and together bring the neuron to threshold. This is:
PREP.explanation: Spatial summation adds postsynaptic potentials arriving at the same time from different synapses. Temporal summation adds potentials arriving in quick succession at the same synapse before the earlier one has decayed. Shunting inhibition reduces the effect of EPSPs by opening conductances near rest. Long-term depression is a lasting weakening of a synapse, not moment-to-moment integration.

PREP.ref: Bear, Connors and Paradiso, somatic sensation
PREP.stem: Which fibres conduct most slowly?
PREP.explanation: Conduction velocity increases with axon diameter and myelination. Unmyelinated C fibres, which carry slow burning pain, temperature and itch, conduct at about 0.5 to 2 m/s. Thinly myelinated A-delta fibres carry fast sharp pain at roughly 5 to 30 m/s, A-beta touch fibres conduct at about 35 to 75 m/s, and large A-alpha fibres at about 80 to 120 m/s. This explains the 'first' sharp and 'second' dull pain after injury.

data.caption: Pain fibres (fast A-delta and slow C fibres) enter through the dorsal root to the dorsal horn, where Melzack and Wall placed the gate. Touch input and signals coming down from the brain can close it; the message then crosses and rises in the spinothalamic tract.

PREP.subject: biological
PREP.stem: Activation of GABA-A receptors usually inhibits a mature neuron because it:
options: Lets chloride in, holding Vm near rest
Blocks calcium entry at the terminal
PREP.explanation: GABA-A receptors are chloride channels; in mature neurons, intracellular chloride is kept low by the KCC2 transporter, so chloride enters and hyperpolarises or clamps the membrane near the chloride equilibrium potential, opposing depolarisation. Opening sodium channels or closing potassium channels would excite. Reduced calcium entry at terminals describes presynaptic GABA-B effects. In immature neurons with high internal chloride (high NKCC1), GABA can depolarise.

data.caption: The GABA-A receptor is a ring of five units round a chloride pore. GABA binds between beta and alpha; benzodiazepines bind at a separate site between alpha and gamma-2 and make the pore open more often, so they need GABA to work. Barbiturates hold it open longer and can open it alone, which is why they are more dangerous.

LONG.subject: statistics
LONG.question: Explain Spearman's rank order correlation. Two judges ranked six dancers as follows: Judge A 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and Judge B 2, 1, 4, 3, 6, 5. Calculate rho and interpret it. When is rho preferred to Pearson's r?
plan: Define rho and when it is used
Comparison with Pearson r, ties and Kendall's tau
LONG.answer:
## Meaning
Spearman's rank order correlation coefficient (rho) measures the strength and direction of association between two sets of ranks. Charles Spearman introduced it. It is Pearson's r applied to ranks, and it assesses whether the relationship is monotonic (consistently increasing or decreasing), not necessarily linear. It ranges from minus 1 to plus 1.

## Formula
When there are no tied ranks: rho = 1 minus (6 times the sum of D squared) / [N (N squared minus 1)], where D is the difference between each pair of ranks and N is the number of pairs.

## Worked calculation
| Dancer | Judge A | Judge B | D | D squared |
| P | 1 | 2 | minus 1 | 1 |
| Q | 2 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| R | 3 | 4 | minus 1 | 1 |
| S | 4 | 3 | 1 | 1 |
| T | 5 | 6 | minus 1 | 1 |
| U | 6 | 5 | 1 | 1 |
| Sum | | | 0 | 6 |
- N = 6, so N (N squared minus 1) = 6 x 35 = 210.
- rho = 1 minus (6 x 6) / 210 = 1 minus 36 / 210 = 1 minus 0.171 = 0.829.

## Interpretation
rho = 0.83 shows strong agreement between the judges: dancers ranked high by one tend to be ranked high by the other, and the judges never differ by more than one place. As an index of inter-judge reliability this is good. For significance, with only six pairs the exact table should be used: the critical value at 0.05 (two-tailed) for N = 6 is 0.886, so rho = 0.83 falls just short. A large-sample t approximation gives p of about 0.04, but this approximation is unreliable with so few pairs. The lesson is that very small samples need very large coefficients to be significant.

## Ties
When two or more scores are tied, each receives the average of the ranks they would occupy: two dancers tied for second and third both receive 2.5. With many ties, the simple formula is inaccurate and Pearson's r should be computed on the ranks.

## When to prefer rho to Pearson's r
| Situation | Use |
| Data are ranks (merit lists, judges' ratings) | rho |
| Ordinal scales such as severity grades | rho |
| Interval data that are badly skewed or have outliers | rho |
| Relationship monotonic but not linear | rho |
| Small samples where normality cannot be assumed | rho |
| Interval or ratio data, linear relationship, roughly normal | Pearson r |
Rho is less affected by outliers because ranks limit the influence of extreme values. When its assumptions hold, Pearson's r is somewhat more powerful because it uses the full information in the scores.

## Kendall's tau
Kendall's tau is another rank correlation, based on the number of concordant and discordant pairs. It handles ties better and has a clearer probabilistic meaning, but is usually smaller in value than rho for the same data.

## Conclusion
Spearman's rho is a simple, robust measure of association for ranked or non-normal data, widely used for inter-rater agreement, item analysis and educational rankings.

LONG.subject: statistics
LONG.question: Write a short note on partial and part (semipartial) correlation.
plan: Define partial correlation with an example
LONG.answer:
## Partial correlation
Partial correlation is the correlation between two variables after the influence of one or more other variables has been removed from both. It answers the question: would X and Y still be related if everyone had the same score on Z?
Example: among school children, shoe size correlates with reading ability, but both depend on age. The partial correlation between shoe size and reading, controlling for age, would be close to zero, showing the original correlation was spurious.
The first-order partial correlation, controlling for one variable Z, is:
r(XY.Z) = [r(XY) minus r(XZ) r(YZ)] / square root of [(1 minus r(XZ) squared)(1 minus r(YZ) squared)].
For instance, if r(XY) = 0.50, r(XZ) = 0.60 and r(YZ) = 0.60, then r(XY.Z) = (0.50 minus 0.36) / (0.64) = 0.22. Much of the X and Y relationship was due to Z.

## Part (semipartial) correlation
Part correlation removes the influence of Z from only one of the two variables, usually the predictor. It shows the unique contribution of X to Y, beyond what Z explains. Its square equals the increase in R squared when X is added to a regression that already contains Z, so it is central to interpreting multiple regression.

## Uses
- Testing whether a correlation is spurious or due to a third variable.
- Examining unique contributions of predictors, such as whether self-efficacy predicts exam marks beyond intelligence.
- Building path and mediation models.
Neither technique proves causation; it only controls for the variables that were measured.

LONG.question: Describe the types of t-tests and their assumptions. Anxiety scores after treatment were: CBT group 12, 14, 11, 15, 13 and wait-list group 18, 16, 17, 19, 15. Test whether the groups differ, calculate the effect size and interpret the result.
plan: Introduce the t distribution and when t is used
What to do when assumptions fail, conclusion
LONG.answer:
## The t distribution
William Gosset, writing as "Student" while working at the Guinness brewery, developed the t distribution for small samples where the population SD is unknown and must be estimated from the sample. The t distribution is symmetrical and bell-shaped like the normal curve but has heavier tails; its exact shape depends on the degrees of freedom, and it approaches the normal curve as samples grow.

## Types of t-test
- One-sample t-test: compares a sample mean with a known or hypothesised population value. Example: is the mean IQ of a group of children different from 100?
- Independent samples t-test: compares the means of two separate groups. Example: CBT versus wait-list.
- Paired (dependent) samples t-test: compares two means from the same or matched people, such as pre and post scores.

## Assumptions
- The DV is measured on an interval or ratio scale.
- Scores are approximately normally distributed in each population (less critical with larger samples).
- Observations are independent (for the independent test, the groups are unrelated).
- Homogeneity of variance: the two populations have equal variances, checked with Levene's test. If violated, Welch's t-test, which does not pool variances, is used.

## Worked independent t-test
H0: the population means are equal. H1: they differ (two-tailed), alpha = 0.05.
| Statistic | CBT | Wait-list |
| N | 5 | 5 |
| Mean | 13 | 17 |
| Sum of squared deviations | 10 | 10 |
| Variance (SS / (N minus 1)) | 2.5 | 2.5 |
- Pooled variance = (10 + 10) / (5 + 5 minus 2) = 20 / 8 = 2.5.
- Standard error of the difference = square root of [2.5 (1/5 + 1/5)] = square root of 1.0 = 1.0.
- t = (13 minus 17) / 1.0 = minus 4.0.
- Degrees of freedom = 5 + 5 minus 2 = 8.
- Critical t at 0.05, two-tailed, df 8 = 2.306. Since the absolute value 4.0 exceeds 2.306, H0 is rejected. The exact p is about 0.004.

## Effect size
Cohen's d = mean difference / pooled SD = 4 / square root of 2.5 = 4 / 1.58 = 2.53. This is a very large effect (Cohen's guide: 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large). Such a large d is typical of tiny invented examples; real therapy trials usually find d of about 0.5 to 0.8 against wait-list.

## Report
The CBT group (M = 13.0, SD = 1.58) reported lower anxiety than the wait-list group (M = 17.0, SD = 1.58), t(8) = minus 4.00, p = .004, d = 2.53.

## Interpretation and cautions
After treatment, the CBT group was significantly less anxious than the wait-list group. Because participants were (we assume) randomly assigned, the difference can be attributed to treatment. But with five people per group, the estimate is imprecise, the normality assumption cannot really be checked, and a wait-list control does not rule out expectancy and attention effects.

## Confidence interval for the difference
The 95 percent confidence interval for the mean difference is the difference plus or minus the critical t times the SE: 4 plus or minus 2.306 x 1.0, that is 1.69 to 6.31 points. Because the interval does not include zero, it agrees with the significant t-test, and it also shows the plausible size of the benefit, which a p value alone does not.

## One-sample and paired versions in brief
In a one-sample test, t = (sample mean minus hypothesised mean) / (SD / square root of N), with N minus 1 df. If 25 children have a mean IQ of 106 and SD 10, t = 6 / 2 = 3.0 with 24 df, which exceeds the critical value of 2.064, so the group differs from 100. The paired test applies the same formula to difference scores.

## When assumptions fail
- Unequal variances: Welch's t-test.
- Non-normal data with small samples, or ordinal data: the Mann Whitney U test (independent) or the Wilcoxon signed rank test (paired).
- More than two groups: ANOVA, because many t-tests inflate the Type I error.

## Conclusion
The t-test is the standard way to compare two means. A full answer chooses the right type, checks assumptions, reports t, df, p and an effect size, and interprets the result in the light of the design.

LONG.subject: biological
LONG.question: Describe the structural and functional methods of studying the living human brain. Compare their principles, strengths and limitations, and discuss their uses in psychology and psychiatry.
plan: Electrical and magnetic methods: EEG, ERP, MEG
LONG.answer:
## Why imaging matters
For most of history the brain could be studied only after death or through the effects of injury, as with Phineas Gage or Broca's patient. Since the 1970s, imaging has allowed us to see the structure and activity of the living brain, linking mind and behaviour to brain systems and helping diagnose neurological causes of psychiatric symptoms.

## Structural methods
1. Computerised tomography, CT: X rays are passed through the head from many angles, and a computer builds cross sectional images. Bone appears white, cerebrospinal fluid dark. CT is fast, cheap and widely available in Indian district hospitals, and is good for detecting bleeding, fractures, large strokes and tumours. It uses ionising radiation and gives poor contrast between grey and white matter. In 1976 Eve Johnstone and colleagues used CT to show enlarged lateral ventricles in schizophrenia.
2. Magnetic resonance imaging, MRI: a strong magnetic field aligns hydrogen nuclei in water; radio pulses knock them out of alignment and the signals they give as they realign are used to build images. Different sequences, such as T1, T2 and FLAIR, highlight anatomy, fluid or lesions. MRI gives excellent soft tissue detail without radiation, but is expensive, slow, noisy and unsuitable for people with pacemakers or metal implants. Volumetric analysis measures structures such as the hippocampus.
3. Diffusion tensor imaging, DTI: a form of MRI that measures the direction of water diffusion along axons. Fractional anisotropy indicates the integrity of white matter tracts, allowing tractography of pathways such as the arcuate fasciculus. Reduced integrity is reported in schizophrenia and after head injury.

## Functional methods
1. Positron emission tomography, PET: a radioactive tracer that emits positrons is injected. Fluorodeoxyglucose shows glucose metabolism; ligands such as raclopride show dopamine D2 receptor availability; amyloid tracers show Alzheimer's plaques. PET measures neurochemistry directly but uses radiation, needs a cyclotron, is costly and has poor temporal resolution of about a minute.
2. Single photon emission computed tomography, SPECT: uses longer lived tracers to measure blood flow or receptors, cheaper than PET but with lower resolution. DaT scans help distinguish Parkinson's disease and Lewy body dementia.
3. Functional MRI, fMRI: measures the blood oxygen level dependent, BOLD, signal. Active neurons increase blood flow more than oxygen use, so oxygenated blood rises locally, changing the magnetic signal. It is non invasive with good spatial resolution of a few millimetres, but temporal resolution is limited to seconds because the blood flow response is slow. Resting state fMRI studies networks such as the default mode network.

## Electrical and magnetic methods
1. Electroencephalography, EEG: electrodes on the scalp, placed by the 10 20 system, record the summed electrical activity of cortical neurons. It has excellent temporal resolution, in milliseconds, is cheap and portable, but poor spatial resolution. It is essential for epilepsy, sleep studies and delirium.
2. Event related potentials, ERPs: averaged EEG responses to repeated stimuli, such as the P300 wave to an odd stimulus or mismatch negativity, which is reduced in schizophrenia.
3. Magnetoencephalography, MEG: measures the tiny magnetic fields produced by neural currents, with millisecond timing and better localisation than EEG, but very expensive and rare in India.

## Comparison
| Method | Measures | Spatial resolution | Temporal resolution | Invasiveness |
| CT | Structure, density | Moderate | Not applicable | X rays |
| MRI | Structure | High | Not applicable | None |
| DTI | White matter tracts | Moderate | Not applicable | None |
| PET | Metabolism, receptors | Moderate | Minutes | Radioactive tracer |
| SPECT | Blood flow, receptors | Low | Minutes | Radioactive tracer |
| fMRI | Blood oxygen changes | High, millimetres | Seconds | None |
| EEG and ERP | Electrical activity | Low | Milliseconds | None |
| MEG | Magnetic fields | Moderate to high | Milliseconds | None |
Methods are often combined, such as simultaneous EEG and fMRI, to get both timing and location.

## Uses
- Research: mapping language, memory, emotion and decision making; studying development and ageing; testing theories, such as the role of the amygdala in fear.
- Psychiatry: ruling out organic causes, such as tumours, strokes or hydrocephalus, in first episode psychosis or late onset depression; diagnosing dementias; PET to study dopamine in schizophrenia and drug occupancy of receptors.
- Neurosurgery: localising language before epilepsy surgery.
- Treatment research: predicting response to treatment, guiding brain stimulation.

## Limitations
- Imaging shows correlation, not causation.
- Group differences in psychiatric disorders are small and overlap with healthy people, so imaging cannot yet diagnose schizophrenia or depression in an individual.
- Many early studies had small samples and false positives; large consortia, such as ENIGMA, now pool thousands of scans.
- Reverse inference, concluding a mental state from activation of a region, is risky because each region serves many functions.
- Cost and access limit use in India, especially MRI and PET outside major cities.

## Conclusion
Each method trades off spatial detail, timing, cost and safety. Together they have transformed knowledge of brain and behaviour, but in psychiatry they remain mainly research tools and a way to exclude other causes.

LONG.subject: biological
LONG.question: Explain the principle of functional magnetic resonance imaging. Describe common study designs and the main limitations in interpreting fMRI findings.
LONG.answer:
## The BOLD signal
Functional MRI detects changes in blood oxygenation that follow neural activity. Oxygenated and deoxygenated haemoglobin have different magnetic properties: deoxyhaemoglobin distorts the magnetic field and lowers the MRI signal. When a brain region becomes active, local blood flow increases more than oxygen consumption, so the proportion of oxygenated blood rises and the signal increases. This blood oxygen level dependent, or BOLD, contrast was described by Seiji Ogawa in 1990.

## The haemodynamic response
The BOLD signal rises about two seconds after a brief neural event, peaks at around five to six seconds and returns to baseline after about 15 to 20 seconds, sometimes with a small undershoot. fMRI therefore has good spatial resolution, a few millimetres, but poor temporal resolution compared with EEG.

## Study designs
1. Block design: alternating periods of a task, such as viewing faces, and a control, such as viewing houses, each lasting about 20 to 30 seconds. Strong signal, simple analysis.
2. Event related design: brief, randomised trials, allowing responses to individual events, such as correct and error trials, to be separated.
3. Resting state: the person lies quietly, and correlations between regions reveal intrinsic networks, such as the default mode network, active during mind wandering, and the salience and central executive networks.
4. Subtraction logic: activity in the control condition is subtracted from the task condition to isolate the process of interest.

## Analysis
Images are corrected for head motion, aligned to a standard brain and smoothed. Statistical tests are run at tens of thousands of voxels, so correction for multiple comparisons is essential.

## Limitations
- Multiple comparisons: in a famous demonstration, researchers found apparent activation in a dead salmon shown photographs when they did not correct their statistics.
- Reverse inference: activation of the amygdala does not prove fear, since the region serves many functions.
- BOLD is an indirect, relative measure of neural activity, influenced by blood vessels, medication, caffeine and age.
- Subtraction assumes that adding a process does not change other processes.
- Small samples produce unreliable findings; test retest reliability of individual task activations is often low.
- The scanner is an artificial setting, and people with claustrophobia, metal implants or severe illness may be excluded.

## Conclusion
fMRI is a powerful, non invasive way to map brain activity, but its findings require careful design, correction and interpretation.

symptoms.line: Loose stools with tummy cramps.

symptoms.label: Can't hold attention
symptoms.line: Drifts off mid-sentence, unaware of the room.

symptoms.label: Came on fast, comes and goes
symptoms.line: Began over hours to days and changes through the day.

symptoms.label: Disoriented
symptoms.line: Unsure of the day, the place or the people.

symptoms.label: Memory decline
symptoms.line: Forgets recent talks and repeats questions.

symptoms.label: Word-finding trouble
symptoms.line: Can't find the names of everyday things.

symptoms.label: Gets lost in familiar places
symptoms.line: Lost on the way home from the market.

symptoms.label: Needs help with daily tasks
symptoms.line: Can no longer manage money, medicines or cooking alone.

symptoms.label: Low self-esteem
symptoms.line: Has long seen themselves as not good enough.

symptoms.label: Hopelessness
symptoms.line: Expects nothing to get better.

symptoms.label: Low for two years or more
symptoms.line: Down on most days for years, never well for long.

ruleOuts.label: Overactive thyroid
ruleOuts.line: Too much thyroid hormone brings anxiety, a racing heart, weight loss and poor sleep.

ruleOuts.label: Underactive thyroid
ruleOuts.line: Low thyroid hormone brings low mood, tiredness, weight gain and slowing.

ruleOuts.label: Stimulant or cannabis use
ruleOuts.line: Cannabis, amphetamines and cocaine can cause psychosis, mania or panic.

ruleOuts.label: High-dose steroid medicine
ruleOuts.line: Steroids like prednisolone can bring on mania, depression or psychosis.

ruleOuts.label: A past manic episode
ruleOuts.line: Depression in someone who has had mania is bipolar depression, not a depressive disorder.

ruleOuts.label: Psychosis only during mood episodes
ruleOuts.line: If the psychosis only ever comes with severe mood episodes, think of a mood disorder with psychotic features.

ruleOuts.label: Clouded consciousness (delirium)
ruleOuts.line: Hallucinations in a confused, drowsy person point to delirium and a medical cause.

ruleOuts.label: A head injury explains it
ruleOuts.line: Concussion can cause poor concentration, irritability and sleep problems.

ruleOuts.label: They are tics, not compulsions
ruleOuts.line: Tics are sudden urges to move without an obsession behind them.

ruleOuts.label: Low blood sugar spells
ruleOuts.line: Sweating, shaking and a pounding heart when sugar drops can look like panic.

ruleOuts.label: Too much caffeine
ruleOuts.line: Many cups of coffee or energy drinks bring jitteriness, worry and poor sleep.

ruleOuts.label: Fear centres on one body flaw
ruleOuts.line: If the dread is about a feature they think looks ugly, think of body dysmorphic disorder.

ruleOuts.label: Avoids people from a fixed belief of harm
ruleOuts.line: Keeping away because others are plotting is psychosis, not social anxiety.

ruleOuts.label: Poor hearing or eyesight
ruleOuts.line: A child who can't hear the teacher or see the board looks inattentive.

ruleOuts.label: Too little sleep
ruleOuts.line: Snoring, late screens or a crowded room at night can cause poor focus and restlessness in a child.

ruleOuts.label: Stopped sleeping pills suddenly
ruleOuts.line: Benzodiazepine withdrawal brings tremor, sweating, poor sleep and fits, much like alcohol withdrawal.

ruleOuts.label: A stomach infection
ruleOuts.line: Food poisoning brings nausea, cramps, aches and diarrhoea.

ruleOuts.label: A viral fever
ruleOuts.line: Flu brings aches, a runny nose, sweats and poor sleep.

ruleOuts.label: A slow decline over years
ruleOuts.line: Memory loss that crept in over years, with steady attention and a clear mind, points to dementia, not delirium.

ruleOuts.label: Depression explains the forgetting
ruleOuts.line: Low mood can slow thinking and memory; it lifts when the depression is treated.

ruleOuts.label: Low vitamin B12 or thyroid
ruleOuts.line: Treatable lacks of B12 or thyroid hormone can cause memory loss and slowing.

clear.label: Tests come back normal
clear.line: History, examination and tests clear the rule-out against you.

diagnoses.name: Major depressive episode
diagnoses.rule: 5 symptoms, one of them low mood or loss of interest.

diagnoses.name: Manic episode
diagnoses.rule: Elevated or irritable mood plus 3 more.

diagnoses.name: Generalised anxiety disorder
diagnoses.rule: Hard-to-control worry plus 3 of the six body and mind symptoms.

diagnoses.name: Panic disorder
diagnoses.rule: Unexpected attacks plus 3 more, including the dread of the next one or its symptoms.

diagnoses.name: Schizophrenia
diagnoses.rule: 3 cards, at least one of delusions, hallucinations or disorganised speech.

diagnoses.name: Obsessive-compulsive disorder
diagnoses.rule: Obsessions or compulsions, plus rituals that eat up time.

diagnoses.name: Social anxiety disorder
diagnoses.rule: Fear of being judged plus 2 more: avoidance, dread beforehand or body signs in company.

diagnoses.name: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder
diagnoses.rule: Inattention or hyperactivity, plus one more sign, starting before 12 and seen in two settings.

diagnoses.name: Alcohol withdrawal
diagnoses.rule: Stopping heavy drinking plus 2 signs, such as a tremor, sweating, poor sleep or nausea.

diagnoses.name: Opioid withdrawal
diagnoses.rule: Stopping or cutting opioids plus 3 signs, such as aches, a runny nose, nausea or yawning.

diagnoses.name: Delirium
diagnoses.rule: Disturbed attention that came on fast and fluctuates, plus one more change in thinking or perception.

diagnoses.name: Major neurocognitive disorder (dementia)
diagnoses.rule: A clear decline in memory, language or finding the way, bad enough to need help with daily life, plus one more.

diagnoses.name: Persistent depressive disorder
diagnoses.rule: Low mood on most days for two years, plus 2 more.
